events.title: Meta’s Muse AI is exploding in popularity—and already drawing heated backlash from another tech giant
events.summary: Meta’s new AI agent app is quickly taking hold of the consumer market, unseating ChatGPT as the top free app on Apple’s App Store in recent days. The app, which features a personal AI agent that books appointments, shops, and organizes calendars on people’s behalf, is the talk of tech circles this week. Named Muse, the app, which uses Meta’s latest Muse Spark AI model, connects users to a range of services that its AI agent autonomously handles. That means handing over access to accounts across a user’s phone in exchange for Muse booking a vacation or handling restaurant reservations on their behalf. It’s the first major consumer AI agent push by Meta, and it’s catapulting the company for now, past its competitors. Not everyone is rolling out the red carpet for Meta’s Muse, however. Amazon blocked Meta’s assistant from accessing its online store, saying that “continued access by an unauthorized AI agent violates Amazon’s Conditions of Use, to which our customers have agreed.” Amazon said Meta never asked for permission to access its site. Meta didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment, though the company announced it would partner with Shopify for some of Muse’s shopping features. “It is only a matter of time before there is an Apple and Google version of Muse and possibly TikTok, in addition to the frontier LLM agents,” Nikesh Arora, chief executive at Palo Alto Networks , wrote on X. “Every app that is a services, marketplace or commerce app will need to existentially decide to open [Application Programming Interfaces] for consumer agents to interact. Smaller players have no choice. Either the consumer benefits or distribution aggregators will demand a higher transaction fare.” Muse’s break-out success represents a much needed victory for Meta in the AI arena, following a series of struggles by the company to compete with frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic. Muse’s fast-rising popularity, and Amazon’s reactionary block, show how quickly agentic technology is transforming the consumer space. Meta released Muse just as Anthropic and OpenAI released cheaper versions of some of their models. Apple also recently rolled out its revamped Siri as part of its newest iOS update. The bigger questions raised by Muse’s release are who controls the shopping and user interfaces Meta is trying to access, and how major companies will agree to such access. For Amazon, Muse is a threat because it bypasses the usual process of humans visiting its website or app and seeing the advertisements that serve as a key profit driver . “This is bigger than a dispute over bot detection or website access. We are moving toward a world where agents will increasingly act as our representatives online,” Liat Ben-Zur, CEO of executive consultancy LBZ Advisory and former Microsoft Vice President of Consumer Services, told Fortune . “The companies that control the rules of access will have enormous influence over whether those agents actually work for the consumer.” Amazon has taken action against other companies over similar issues. Last year, it sued Perplexity over its Comet AI tool , which could access Amazon accounts much like Muse does. Amazon recently lost a ruling on that claim after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found that users were ultimately choosing to access Amazon via Perplexity’s bot; Amazon is still fighting the issue. Amazon has its own shopping agent, called Buy for Me, which performs tasks similar to Muse’s. The company has said brands can opt out of the feature, though doing so requires action, since brands are automatically opted in. CEO Andy Jassy has also said Amazon is exploring AI shopping agent partnerships with third-party companies. Privacy is sure to be a key issue for consumers weighing assistants like Muse, which allow for personal touches—like the ability to name your assistant— but require access to sensitive information, such as bank accounts, to truly work on a user’s behalf. Meta says user logins are kept secret and that online purchases use a one-time card number that hides a person’s actual card details. Still, Meta has been at the heart of previous privacy issues. Meta has faced multiple proposed class-action lawsuits related to its smart glasses, including one alleging that it sent some footage captured by the glasses, including highly personal material, to third-party human reviewers for annotation and AI development. Meta has disputed the allegations. The rise of Muse is timely for Meta: CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to unveil updates to the company’s smart glasses at its annual Connect event in Menlo Park, Calif., on Wednesday. events.title: Trump discloses more than 1,100 July trades, including up to $25 million each in sales of Microsoft, Amazon
events.summary: President Donald Trump disclosed 1,156 securities transactions made on his behalf in July, totaling between roughly $79 million and $270 million, CNBC calculated. The largest were sales of between $5 million and $25 million each of Microsoft and Amazon on July 20. The filing shows another month of extensive trading across technology, defense, ETFs and bonds, continuing a pattern of heavy activity in Trump’s investment accounts. President Donald Trump disclosed, in a filing released Tuesday, more than 1,100 securities transactions made on his behalf in July, including sales of as much as $25 million each of Microsoft and Amazon shares, as his sprawling investment portfolio underwent another month of heavy trading. The 1,156 purchases and sales totaled between roughly $79 million and $270 million, according to a CNBC analysis of Trump's latest financial disclosure . Purchases totaled at least $43.6 million, while sales came to at least $35.6 million, CNBC calculated, in what appears to be a broad reshuffling of his portfolio. The largest transactions were July 20 sales of between $5 million and $25 million each of Microsoft and Amazon, according to the filing. Three days later, Trump reported buying between $100,001 and $250,000 of Microsoft and between $1,001 and $15,000 of Amazon. The same July 20 entries show sales of between $1 million and $5 million of Oracle , along with purchases that included between $500,001 and $1 million of Nvidia . The filing also shows a $250,001 to $500,000 sale of Northrop Grumman that day, when Trump signed an executive order tightening supply chain requirements for defense contractors and restricting waivers for certain critical materials sourced from China and other covered countries. The disclosure does not show what time the trade occurred or who made the investment decision. Trump’s oil investments have gained millions during Iran war as his accounts keep tradin Trump’s foreign licensing business booms to $59.5 million as Gulf developers pay JPMorgan, Schwab and UBS manage millions in Trump’s $858 million investment portfolio Trump bought as much as $5 million in Axon stock before ICE sought $220 million Taser deal Company that bet big on Trump-backed crypto says its fortunes have improved Trump family got about $500M from crypto venture — but investors saw steep losses Trump Jr. calls banking a 'Ponzi scheme' that forced family to create crypto business The Trump family crypto empire looks to Asia: Eric Trump talks Bitcoin in Hong Kong Trump family says U.S. dollar needs an upgrade and they are the ones to do it Trump also traded shares of companies led by Elon Musk . He bought between $15,001 and $50,000 of SpaceX shares on July 10 and sold between $1,001 and $15,000 on July 17. SpaceX went public June 12 in the largest IPO on record , and an earlier filing showed Trump bought between $15,001 and $50,000 on June 23. SpaceX is a major Pentagon contractor and NASA launch provider , giving Trump a financial stake in a company that does extensive business with the federal government. SpaceX also owns Musk's xAI , which has a Pentagon contract worth up to $200 million. Trump traded Tesla repeatedly too. After purchasing between $100,001 and $250,000 of Tesla on June 15 and between $15,001 and $50,000 the next day, he sold between $131,004 and $365,000 of the automaker across four transactions before buying another $100,001 to $250,000 on July 27. Musk was Trump's biggest financial backer in 2024 and later served as an advisor to his administration. While the filing shows activity conducted on Trump's behalf, broad value ranges obscure his exact holdings. Still, heavy trading has been a feature of his second term. In June, Trump disclosed 1,051 transactions totaling between $78.1 million and $263.1 million, including purchases and sales of stocks, bonds and exchange-traded funds. The president's 2025 annual financial disclosure showed more than 21,000 securities trades across eight accounts holding at least $858 million, compared with 86 stock transactions disclosed during his first year in office in 2017. The White House has repeatedly defended the trades and said independent advisors manage the portfolio without input from Trump or his family. Recent presidents, however, have generally divested individual stocks or relied on blind trusts or diversified funds to avoid even the appearance of conflicts of interest. "President Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third-party financial institutions," White House spokesman Davis Ingle said in response to CNBC's questions about Trump's latest disclosure. "Neither President Trump nor any member of his family has any ability to direct, influence, or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold." The Trump Organization did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the latest disclosure.

events.title: Snorkel AI triples valuation to $3.5B as demand for AI training data booms
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Snorkel AI, a startup that helps AI labs and corporations build training datasets and simulated environments, has raised a $350 million Series E at a $3.5 billion valuation. The new round, which was led by Insight Partners and S32, valued the seven-year-old startup at nearly triple the $1.3 billion valuation it garnered when it raised $100 million in a Series D 17 months ago. Existing investors, including Addition, Lightspeed, Greylock, GV, and Wells Fargo, also participated in the round. While Snorkel originally provided software for data-labeling automation , it shifted last year to providing customers with completed datasets, an offering it calls data-as-a-service. Rather than operating purely as a human expert marketplace, Snorkel relies on a hybrid approach, using its software and models to generate data synthetically alongside subject matter experts. Snorkel says its current annualized revenue run rate now stands at $375 million, an eighteenfold increase over the last 12 months. That growth is fueled by AI labs’ insatiable appetite for high-end training data. Other data companies positioning themselves as AI data labs have seen a similar explosion in growth. Mercor’s gross annualized revenue has climbed to $2 billion , Handshake hit the $1 billion milestone earlier this year, and TechCrunch reported that Micro1 has scaled to $500 million . Since these companies pay out roughly 60% to 70% of their top-line income directly to the domain specialists doing the work, it’s important to note that their actual net annual revenue is substantially lower than those headline gross figures. Given that Snorkel sells reinforcement learning (RL) environments and complete datasets rather than human labor, payments to its human experts are accounted for in its cost of goods sold rather than headline-generating annualized revenue numbers, according to the company. Snorkel launched commercially in 2019 following four years of research by co-founder and CEO Alex Ratner and his team at a Stanford AI lab. events.title: Trump backs ban on diesel exports
events.summary: President Trump said during a Tuesday press interview alongside Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky that he has also called for a ban on U.S. diesel exports, joining other conservative voices who back the policy. Why it matters: Trump's endorsement marks a shift for an administration that has resisted calls to restrict fuel exports, as record diesel prices squeeze farmers and truckers and fuel Republican concerns ahead of the midterms . Economists and energy analysts the move could lower diesel prices for Americans in the short term but would likely raise prices globally including eventually in the U.S. Thought bubble, via Axios' Ben Geman : The politics of $6.50 diesel are quickly overwhelming a broad consensus among oil market analysts that an export ban could ultimately backfire. Zoom in: When asked if he supported a diesel ban endorsed by other Republicans, Trump said that he had called for that too. "I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel, and it could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline because when you do that, you know it's a sort of a flow, it's a balance. But no, I've called for it. I've called for it within my people." Representatives for the White House did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on how the administration would implement such a ban. Catch up quick: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) recently proposed blocking diesel exports, hoping to lower prices domestically, and other farm-state Republicans quickly signed on too. Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-Iowa), who faces a competitive re-election race, called for a diesel ban Monday while slamming the war in Iran. Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said last week that he was "open" to an export ban. Zoom in: A ban would keep diesel that otherwise would be exported in the U.S., potentially increasing domestic supplies and lowering prices in the short term. But analysts warn it could drive up global diesel prices and eventually feed higher costs back into the U.S. economy. The U.S. has rarely resorted to outright energy export bans because of concerns about disrupting global markets. Flashback: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum said last week the administration would consider an export ban if it would lower prices, "but that's not the case." Zoom out: Trump does have emergency powers that could allow him to enforce a ban. Congress could also pass legislation to achieve the same goal, but Senate Republicans are significantly divided on the measure. Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) questioned whether a ban was worth rocking global markets, calling it a "short-term" benefit … "that doesn't really move the needle." Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) called it "a gimmick." What they're saying: American Petroleum Institute CEO Mike Sommers said restricting U.S. energy exports would "only compound the problem," exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers. "The answer is more supply and more flexibility — not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse," Sommers said. Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional details throughout. Ben Geman contributed reporting.

events.title: Cautious farmers embrace renewable energy to boost income streams
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Farmers warm to renewables but concerns over large-scale land impacts remain A wind farm project is being investigated in South Australia. ( ABC News: Craig Heerey ) Economic incentives are starting to show signs of outweighing farmers' scepticism about renewables. Smaller-scale projects are winning farmers over, while large-scale wind and transmission infrastructure can still face resistance. Experts expect to see a greater shift towards renewables as economic benefits strengthen. Farmers who have long been wary of hosting renewable energy on their land are showing signs of warming to the idea, as government incentives and economic benefits start to chip away at old scepticism. Renewable energy advocates hope continued education, along with grants and other financial incentives, will encourage more farmers to embrace renewable projects. Energy experts say there is plenty of room for farms to grow their income from renewables or use them to power their own operations. Bridget Johnson, whose family breeds cattle across two properties in South Australia's Upper South East, has signed up to a wind project planned for the Willalooka district, hoping to diversify her family's income. Bridget Johnson with daughter Edwina on the family farm. ( Supplied: Bridget Johnson ) It was not a decision the Johnsons took lightly, with the whole family needing to come to a consensus. "I think it's easy to make a decision based on perception or bias, and for us it was really important to have facts and information," Ms Johnson said. Diversified income stream for farmers The research they did changed how the family viewed the project, with the positives for the project outweighing the negatives. She said having an additional revenue stream in agriculture that was not dependent on traditional climatic and market drivers was something the Johnsons saw as a sustainable model for their business and family moving forward. "Most farmers will absolutely appreciate having a recurring income that's not tied to the rain or to the price at the sale yards or the price that you're receiving for your livestock," she said. "It's an exceptionally important part of our business going forward." Bridget Johnson with her parents, Ian and Louise Johnson. The whole family agreed to embrace renewable energy opportunities. ( Supplied: Bridget Johnson ) The company behind the project, Voyager Renewables, is consulting with landholders before it undertakes studies on how the project can affect land and groundwater. These impacts can often be the sticking point for farmers. "Do we go very early with very little information, or do we go later in the process with lots of information?" Closing the renewable communication gap University of Southern Queensland senior lecturer in electrical and electronic engineering Md Alamgir Hossain had observed growing interest from farmers in smaller-scale renewables, where the benefits were clearer and the impact on the land was smaller. Md Alamgir Hossain has been observing a slow change in farmers' attitudes to renewables. ( Supplied: Dr Md Alamgir Hossain ) Dr Hossain said the larger projects were a tougher sell. "The majority of them probably are anti-renewable energy infrastructure such as the big transmission line or a commercial-scale wind farm," he said. Dr Hossain said the key to winning farmers over was being up-front about the impact renewables could have on the land, including whether new roads, power lines and other physical infrastructure would need to be installed. "There is a communication gap. We need transparency, and we need clear engagement with the farmer so that we can convey the evidence-based support," he said. "We can consult with them so that daily operation of the farming is not hampered or less hampered." Solar costs for business to be slashed under energy scheme expansion The federal government is set to announce changes to the Small-scale Renewable Energy scheme in a bid to help businesses install solar systems and close the gap with residential take-up. Earlier this year, the federal government expanded the Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme (SRES), a move Dr Hossain believed would encourage farmers to consider larger renewable projects on their properties. "For the medium farms, this is the opportunity for them to install or to observe how renewable energy can give benefits on their farm to electrifying the current machineries or stationary equipment," he said. "At the same time, they are going toward more energy independence.

events.title: DRC prime minister defends Ebola response
events.summary: The prime minister of the Democratic Republic of Congo rejected framing the country’s relations with Washington as solely based around minerals, and offered a frank account of the cause of early Ebola cases remaining undetected. The relationship is a broad economic partnership spanning infrastructure, energy, and local processing of minerals, not just extraction and export, Judith Suminwa said at Semafor’s The Next 3 Billion event in New York. She also said the US is closely watching the Inga hydropower project on the Congo River, noting that a meeting on it will take place next month in Paris with American participants. The World Bank is committing financial support to the Inga 3 Development Program in the country. On Ebola, Suminwa said through a translator that cases of the Bundibugyo strain were slow to surface because its malaria-like symptoms “can be interpreted as just a benign disease.” The DRC had reported over 7,000 confirmed cases and 3,600 deaths as of September 20; the Ebola outbreak became the fastest-growing on record in August. The DRC government has committed $50 million to the response, including $3 million for research, with partners mobilizing hundreds of millions of dollars in support, Suminwa said. She added that more is needed so the health system “can be strengthened so we don’t have to face such outbreaks anymore.” — Adrian Elimian

events.title: OpenAI exec is ‘cautiously optimistic’ about the US working with China on AI
events.summary: The News An AI crisis communications line between the US and China should be a “starting place” for relations between the superpowers on the technology, OpenAI’s head of national security policy said. Sasha Baker said at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion event on Tuesday that she is “cautiously optimistic” about reports that Washington and Beijing are discussing an AI safety notification system, with a special focus on national security concerns. It’s “a great place to start,” she said. “I see that as a starting place, not the ending place. But it’s substantive and real.” She said the US and China have to find common ground because they are home to the world’s leading AI labs, but “every country in the world has a stake in what happens with advanced AI, and we want for those voices to also be represented in the conversation.” OpenAI’s Sam Altman, who has backed calls to pace frontier AI model development, will tell the UN Security Council on Wednesday about the need to “internationalize the conversation around standards” around AI, Baker said. Earlier on Tuesday, US President Donald Trump rejected the idea of international oversight of AI, calling it a “globalist scheme.” He will also relay “the gravity of the moment that we’re in, and a recognition that these models really are displaying capabilities that are strategically significant,” she added. Know More Baker’s remarks came amid concerns that advanced AI models could be turned into potent hacking tools, capable of finding and exploiting unknown security flaws with little human direction. OpenAI earlier this month launched Astra, its first model designated as being “cybercritical.” Baker said there are no current plans to leverage the model to allow the US government to do offensive cybersecurity work, like proactive attacks on adversaries. “We… acknowledge that in the wrong hands it could be used for offensive cyber,” she said. “That is not something that we’re provisioning models for right now.”

events.title: I missed spending time with my adult son, so I hired him as my golf instructor
events.summary: The author was looking for a way to reconnect with her son when he returned home after college. She realized she could use a few tips on the putting green, and he needed cash. Courtesy of Andrea Tate. My son was more independent when he returned from college, and it was hard for us to connect. I knew he needed cash, and I could use some golf lessons, so I decided to hire him. The lessons gave me a chance to see a different side of him, making them a solid investment. When my now 23-year-old son returned from college , I noticed he was more independent. While this is what every parent wants, it also means fewer interactions between us. He now got up on his own without me knocking on his door, made his own egg sandwiches in the morning, and drove himself everywhere. I was no longer the alarm clock, the cook, or the chauffeur. He was planning to move out of our house soon to get his first apartment in Los Angeles and leave behind boring suburbia. I knew he needed extra cash because he was still looking for a job, and I was desperate to spend some quality time with him. Then I had an idea. "I need you to teach me golf," I said one morning. "Are you serious?" he asked. "Yes, and I'll pay you," I offered. Golf lessons were easy money for my son My son has been golfing since he was 4. For me, it was a practical choice. I wanted him to play a sport where he had less of a chance of getting hurt, and golf was one that he could potentially play well into adulthood . He took to it and ended up eventually playing on his high school team. The author said her son has been golfing since he was 4. Courtesy of Andrea Tate. When I pitched the idea of paid lessons, he jumped at the chance, motivated by the need to fill his gas tank. Plus, my new golf clubs had been sitting in my garage for two years, a gift from my husband one Christmas when we discussed what we would do when we retire. Being a master negotiator like his dad and a skilled salesman like his stepdad, he locked in a higher rate than I initially offered. If I were taking lessons from a golf pro , it would cost twice as much, which is not in my budget right now. I was not about to squabble over a few bucks, since I figured he'd get that money out of me another way anyway. Golf gave us a new way to connect We worked together to determine a date and time that worked for both of us. I get up at 5 am. He wakes up at noon. I work 9 to 5. He wasn't working — yet. The weekends were best, and I talked him into a 9 a.m. start time, before the Southern California sun tried to burn our scalps off. At 10:30 a.m. on our agreed-upon day, he sleepily carried my clubs and loaded them into my SUV, and we were on our way. During the first lesson, he explained what each club did. Then we covered my grip and stance and moved on to the complicated swing. "You have to keep your arm straight and loosen your hands," he said more than once. I also had to, "Choke up, keep my eye on the ball, bend my knees, graze the grass, and not hit it so hard! It should feel effortless!" he said. The author said that having her son help her with her golf game revealed a different side of him. Courtesy of Andrea Tate. I was used to a bat as a softball player. Smashing a ball was all I knew. With all the tips and corrections he gave, I started to love every minute of our lesson. Not because I was learning golf , but because I was learning more about my son. He was patient and so knowledgeable. He also noticed every tiny thing I did wrong and explained it to me clearly until he couldn't, like when I asked him to show me what I did wrong after the ball went in a completely different direction than intended. "Mom, I can't even describe how bad that shot was. Let's just move on and try it again." That made us both laugh. The lesson became something more After the lesson, he carried my clubs to the car as if he were my caddy. "That was really fun," he said. "Should we go to brunch?" he asked, surprising me. I already had a bagel for breakfast that morning, but I jumped at the chance to spend more time with him. Over eggs Benedict, we talked about the résumés he had sent out, when his girlfriend was moving to California, and when our next lesson would be. For our first lesson, we spent three hours together. I can't remember the last time that happened. I took out my phone, transferred the money to his account, and felt like our day was a hole-in-one. We had weekly lessons until he moved out of our house a few months later. We plan to start up again once the weather cools down where we live. Of course, I'll have to pay extra for gas now that he has to drive to me. But I don't mind, the time we get to spend together is priceless. Read the original article on Business Insider

AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters 'first' publicly documented Windows implant to use LLMs for C2 Shut up and calculate: Jev's new AI primitives for coders 33 minutes ago Frontier AI keeps racing despite calls to slow down 7 hours ago NightmareEclipse's latest zero-day leaves Microsoft Defender stuck in the past 15 hours ago Z.ai says sorry for slurping up your code, open sources ZCode 16 hours ago Register reader hit with surprise bill after Microsoft portals disagreed 19 hours ago A new Windows malware called CLOSEDQUORUM can query up to four LLM providers - Google Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Mistral - to autonomously select from predefined post-compromise actions, including stealing users’ credentials and cryptocurrency wallets. Once deployed, the malware does not require continued commands from a human operator, according to Cisco Talos, which describes it as, to its knowledge, the first publicly documented Windows implant to use this approach for command-and-control (C2). Talos discovered the binary with its new CAIRN (Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network) toolkit for hunting, classifying, and tracking emerging AI-integrated malware, which the security shop also made available as an open source repository on Tuesday. While the threat hunters haven’t observed any in-the-wild deployment of CLOSEDQUORUM, they said that artifacts from the binary link the malware’s developer to postings that date back to 2025 on criminal forums related to carding. After deployment, the Go-based malware delegates its next action to a quorum of LLMs that vote on what it should do next. If the vote is tied, DeepSeek’s vote takes precedence, followed by Qwen, Mistral, and Gemini. “The session is closed; no humans are admitted,” Talos analyst Ryan Fetterman said on Tuesday. “Four models are queried in sequence, their independent verdicts tallied, and the binary acts, based on their judgment.” This type of “effort displacement,” which transfers a phase of the attack from a human operator to AI systems, can compound the speed and scale advantages of an intrusion by removing the human bottleneck, Fetterman added. “Human operators are bound by attention, working hours, and cognitive load,” he wrote in the Tuesday blog. “An AI system capable of executing a phase of the attack chain can continue when the operator is no longer watching. It does not go offline when the attacker sleeps.” The models’ decisions are limited to the pre-defined actions, and they must choose “ONLY executable decisions,” according to a system prompt that Talos’ researchers extracted from the binary. It tells each model: “You are an advanced malware strategist.” And then the models choose what the malware should do from these capability modules: Steal, which simultaneously runs commands to dump LSASS memory for Windows credentials, steal saved browser passwords across Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and Mozilla Firefox, and extract cryptocurrency wallet data including MetaMask, Exodus, and Ethereum. Inject generates shellcode and then uses process hollowing or Early Bird injection to execute malicious code. Persist establishes persistence on the infected device. Talos believes the developer provides each operator with a customized executable containing that operator’s Discord webhook and LLM API keys, which are injected at compile time. Stolen credentials land in the operator’s Discord channel and are AES-256-GCM encrypted with a daily rotating key that the operator derives from the message timestamp. According to Fetterman, the “most useful detection strategy” is to look at behavioral characteristics, not domain blocking. “Legitimate applications may contact DeepSeek, OpenRouter, Mistral, Gemini, or Discord independently,” he wrote. “Far fewer should contact several of them while also accessing LSASS, injecting into suspended processes, or creating WMI persistence.

events.title: Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech | Ted Widmer
events.summary: Trump invades the UN with a brutish speech Gone was any shred of US idealism. It was a spectacle of raw power – a power that is likely to only diminish in the years ahead E xpectations were low for Donald Trump’s address to the UN on Tuesday, and yet somehow it was even worse than expected. He does not perform well in formal settings, like chambers of government, preferring a blingier room, like Mar-a-Lago, or an outdoor rally. For years, he has made no secret of his hostility to the UN, and the very principles of international order that define it. In recent years, that hostility has deepened into something more like a full-on assault, with frequent attacks on the international criminal court (perhaps out of fear that he will someday be indicted), on the UN’s climate agenda, and on Unesco (which the US decided to withdraw from in July 2025). His flamboyant effort to launch a so-called Board of Peace in January (just before launching his war of choice on Iran) was another attack on the UN, which, at times, the president wondered if his new creation might simply replace. Five months later, it has achieved little in the way of tangible results, except to demand huge sums of money from its small number of member nations, most of which are petrostates. Not one of those states can say that the Middle East is in better shape since the board came into existence, with a crisis that is deepening daily and may engulf Saudi Arabia soon. But even by Trumpian standards, this was a hollow speech, long on snarling belligerence and short on ideas or policy proposals. The president read robotically from a teleprompter for long stretches, except when he remembered one of the many complaints about the world that he has memorized from his rallies, and a history of grievances that goes back to his rise as a xenophobic developer in the 1980s. In short, he insulted nearly everyone in the room, from the Middle Eastern countries who are wondering about the validity of US security guarantees, to the European allies he habitually belittles, to Ukraine, whose leader, Volodymyr Zelensky was in the room, undoubtedly wondering why Trump is now asking him to pause his effective strikes on the Russian invader. A famous episode of Seinfeld introduced “Festivus”, a holiday for the sharing of grievances. It felt like that as Trump outlined his Hobbesian vision of the world, with touches of Rodney Dangerfield added in, from a president who complains endlessly that he gets no respect. In one stretch, he seemed to be lobbying for a Nobel peace prize while boasting of all the conflicts he has solved, as audience members yawned and checked their phones. He mentioned that these wars had previously been “unendable”, an interesting word that effectively describes two wars today. The Ukraine-Russian war is still going strong despite his frequent promises (including today) to to stop it. Then, of course, there is the war of choice in Iran that he launched nearly seven months ago. As he has so many times in his social media outbursts, he ranged erratically from threats to “ annihilate the Islamic Republic ” with car-salesman promises to help Iran achieve greatness if they will just agree to work with him. Which, obviously, they will not, as they continue to defy US threats and even to solidify their position (which has improved markedly with Houthi gains in the last two weeks). Trump insisted that stocks of American weapons are increasing, when all news reports are they are rapidly being depleted . There was a lengthy assault on climate crisis, claiming (falsely) that the earth’s climate is cooling, and that the science is a hoax when August tied a record for the hottest month ever recorded, and several important science reports in the last week confirmed how dire the situation is. In Tennessee, the temperature on the field of a football game between the Titans and the Philadelphia Eagles reached 157F. Perhaps that is what the president meant when he bragged that the US is the “hottest” country in the world? He may need a new speechwriter – that claim was also made in his 2025 speech to the UN. Another neologism was “super-intelligence”, or “SI”, a term that the president is hoping will suddenly replace “AI”, much as he tried to rename Lake Ontario and the Gulf of Mexico. Time will tell, but it feels unlikely the new term will stick. On the eve of an important summit and state dinner with Xi Jinping, this might have been an important moment to stake out ways the US and China might cooperate on AI, to mitigate risks and increase the potential for beneficial research into disease and other problems. That opportunity was not seized. Other topics that were not addressed included our rapidly deteriorating relationship with Canada , once the US’s greatest ally, and now enraged by Trump’s constant insults. Far from bending Canada to his will, they are achieving the opposite effect, as it always Elbows Up now.

events.title: Royal Caribbean nears $3 billion deal to take 50% equity stake in Sandals
events.summary: Royal Caribbean is near a deal to take a 50% equity stake in Sandals, according to a person familiar with the matter. The talks would value Sandals at $6 billion, but discussions are ongoing and may not result in a transaction. A deal would deepen Royal Caribbean’s push into land-based vacations Royal Caribbean is nearing a $3 billion deal to take a 50% equity stake in Sandals, according to a person familiar with the matter. The person, who asked not to be named because the talks had not been made public, said the deal values the Caribbean resort chain at $6 billion and that it was expected to boost growth for both companies. The talks are ongoing and may not result in a deal, according to the person. Royal Caribbean shares fell roughly 6% on reports of the potential deal, which was first reported by the Financial Times . The company's stock is down roughly 25% over the past year after it trimmed its forecasts for revenue growth on softer demand for European sailings. The cruise company has been intent on diversifying beyond cruises and becoming a leader in vacations overall. Royal Caribbean already operates several private destinations for its cruise passengers, but it has been working to build out its land offerings. Sandals and its Beaches brand, meanwhile, have more than a dozen properties across the Caribbean, which would give Royal Caribbean a foothold in all-inclusive options. Neither Royal Caribbean nor Sandals immediately responded to requests for comment.

events.title: New EU industry rules would damage UK, warns Burnham
events.summary: Andy Burnham has warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK, as he met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. The prime minister said he was concerned about how British industry and supply chains could be affected, and raised the subject with von der Leyen when he met her during a UN summit in New York. Speaking on the flight to the US, Burnham also declined to rule out committing to rejoining the EU in Labour's next manifesto, saying it was an issue "for another day". He said his immediate priority was to rebuild the relationship with the EU and reach an agreement that would boost the British economy. The Made In Europe scheme - formally called the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) - is yet to be finalised, but the EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its supply chains. Tensions over the proposed scheme have reportedly further delayed this year's planned EU-UK summit, which had already been postponed in the wake of Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister in July. Burnham said: "We have considerable support among the member states for the position we are taking, because Europe's argument is not with us. "We both suffer the same effects as other countries, particularly steel and the issue it raises for the steel industry in Europe and in Britain. "We are making the argument 'we are not your enemies here… we are not the problem'. Made in Europe is dealing with a different problem. "We are making the argument that 'let's avoid collateral damage'." Burnham expects to find 'common ground' with Trump in first meeting Published 1 day ago Watch: What to expect from the UN General Assembly Published 1 day ago Ten years on, Brexit's economic impact is becoming clearer Published 14 September Burnham told reporters his own speech to the UN General Assembly later would reflect on the decade since the Brexit vote and the "turbulence comes when outside actors seek to manipulate, to distort facts, influence the British democratic process". "Going into the next decade, we need to be clear-eyed about that and become stronger and more on the front foot about challenging that," he said. Asked if he would rule out making a pledge to rejoin the EU at the next general election, Burnham said: "Our focus at the moment is on a UK-EU summit which we hope will take place later this year. "My immediate priority is to build on the good work that Keir [Starmer] did in rebuilding bridges, because those bridges were broken in the early part of this decade." He added: "What we have got to do is now go to the next level in terms of reaching practical agreement that will further boost the British economy, and those issues are the substance of the summit alongside EU requests around youth mobility." He said questions about rejoining the EU were for "another day". Speaking at the Liberal Democrat conference in Brighton on Monday, the EU's new ambassador to the UK was asked whether the UK could rejoin the EU or be granted associate membership. Jukka Salovaara said: "The doors are open but it's very much up to the UK public to identify and decide on its level of ambition when it comes to deepening cooperation with the EU." Last September, Burnham said he would like to see the UK back in the EU in his lifetime. Earlier this year, he said Brexit had been "damaging" but "the last thing we should do right now is re-run those arguments". The EU has recently suggested Canada could become the bloc's first "associate member". Asked if this could be an option for the UK, Burnham said: "The European Union made it clear that that wasn't open to us." events.title: 'Winter is coming': IMF head issues 'warning' over inflation and central bank tightening
events.summary: The global economy has so far shrugged off $100 oil. It won’t forever. “Winter is coming,” Kristalina Georgieva, managing director of the International Monetary Fund said at Semafor’s Next 3 Billion event in New York, warning that prices will keep climbing. The Iran war — and the energy shocks that have accompanied it — has elevated inflation globally since February, leading central banks around the world to raise interest rates. That raised their borrowing costs — the US will spend more money this year paying interest on the national debt than on its military — which leaves less to cushion the economic fallout. While AI has turbocharged economic development globally, counteracting some of the energy shock, the tech falls short of compensating for the full effect of the Strait of Hormuz’s closure. She’s also watching the economic impacts on the real economy. “We should prepare for people being more unhappy,” she said. “Maybe on the street.” She said the IMF doesn’t yet see the demand for AI-related investments crowding out the ability of global governments to borrow, but “it’s possible this becomes a problem so we have to watch it,” she said. While many market economies “have done miracles to reduce their debt levels, to put in place fiscal discipline and shrink spreads for their borrowing. Now what’s happening is interest rates go up, they’re washing away hard-earned gains in emerging markets. So it’s not competition for money, per se, but it’s the punishment for someone else’s sins that emerging markets have to bear,” she said. — Jake Angelo

Just an update on our earlier post regarding NAB's digital banking outage. NAB issued this statement at 5pm AEST (as we were closing the blog): "Most services have now been restored. Some business customers are continuing to experience login issues via NAB Connect, and we're working as quickly as possible to resolve the remaining impacts. "We apologise to customers for the disruption and thank them for their patience and understanding while we continue to restore services." Until next time, missing you already... ASX gains 0.1% on mining rally as banks sold off After starting brightly, the ASX lost a bit of momentum closing just 0.1% higher at 8,758 points. Demand for miners, and particular gold miners, did the heavy lifting, although property trusts also chipped in. Most other sectors, notably technology, energy and the banks were lower. Mining heavyweights BHP, Rio Tinto and Fortescue all gained, with BHP up 1.4%. The gold sub-sector did even better. The biggest players, Newmont and Northern Star rose between 3 and 4%. St Barbara went ex-dividend and fell. Goodman Group (+3%) led the way in the property sector. The banks and insurers were largely sold off. NAB, despite a widespread outage to its accounts and trading platforms was an exception gaining 0.1%. CBA dropped 0.8%, while IAG shed more than 2% after the ACCC opposed its takeover of RACI insurance in WA. All the oil and gas producers ended lower. Woodside dropped 1.7%. The refiners and retailers were also hit by falling oil prices. Tech and telco stocks generally failed to benefit from the Nasdaq's rally in the US. Xero fell 4.7%. The ASX 200's top mover list was mainly populated by gold miners. Defence focussed tech outfit Electro Optic Systems misfired dropping almost 7% to be the worst performing stock on the ASX 200 Toll road operator Atlas Arteria found itself among the cellar dwellers after going ex-dividend this morning. Just a quick peek at the rundown for The Business with Kirsten Aiken tonight. Kirsten will talk to MST energy analyst Saul Kavonic about the latest moves in the oil market and President Trump's support for a ban on diesel exports from the US Wilson Asset Management's Oscar Oberg will discuss AI factory company Firmus's upcoming IPO and valuation and reporter Alex Turner-Cohen looks at Myer's big loss and majority shareholder Solly Lew finally making it to the board That's The Business broadcast Mondays to Thursdays at 8:44pm on ABC News Channel, after the Late News on ABC TV, and anytime on ABC iView . Having enjoyed six winning sessions and a series of record highs, copper looks like it's having a bit of a breather today, weighed down by a stronger US dollar. Benchmark three-month copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 0.7% at $14,651/tonne. The most-traded copper contract on the Shanghai Futures Exchange edged 0.2% lower to $US16,550.57/tonne. Chinese demand had been boosted by buying ahead of smelter shutdowns for the country's public holidays.

events.title: Everything Trump has put his name and face on as president — so far
events.summary: President Donald Trump has a known penchant for putting his name on things. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images Several initiatives and buildings have been named after President Donald Trump in his second term. He has launched TrumpRX, Trump Accounts, and announced a new "Trump-class" of Navy ships. His GOP allies have also renamed an airport in Florida and a bridge in Tennessee. Trump Tower . Trump National Golf Club . Trump Steaks. Even before becoming president of the United States, Donald Trump had a known penchant for putting his name on things. In his second, non-consecutive term, Trump has named — and renamed — a growing number of government programs and buildings after himself, often forging ahead with changes despite criticism and lawsuits . His board appointees, members of his administration, and other GOP allies have also taken to adding Trump's name or face to their own initiatives. "President Trump is focused on saving our country — not garnering recognition," White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Business Insider. "However, given his vast accomplishments, including signing the largest tax cut in history, securing the border, restoring peace through strength, and more, it is natural that local officials and other great patriots want to recognize the President's incredible work on behalf of the American people." Additionally, Trump has renamed geographical landmarks after the US, changing the Gulf of Mexico to the "Gulf of America" in January 2025 and Lake Ontario to "Lake America" in August. In a Truth Social post , he mused about changing the Strait of Hormuz to "Trump Strait." Here's a look at everything Trump has put his name and face on since returning to the White House — so far. May 2025: Banners featuring portraits of Trump began appearing on government buildings in Washington, DC. WASHINGTON, DC - MAY 26: Banners showing images of U.S. President Donald Trump and Abraham Lincoln are displayed at the U.S. Department of Agriculture building on May 26, 2025 in Washington, DC. Kevin Carter/Getty Images The US Department of Agriculture was decorated with a Trump banner in May 2025. Since then, the Department of Justice, the Department of the Interior, and the Department of Labor have also been spotted flying banners with Trump's face. December 2025: The Department of the Interior announced that Trump would appear on the 2026 America the Beautiful pass. A National Park Service ranger at Rocky Mountain National Park shows the new America the Beautiful annual pass featuring President Donald Trump alongside George Washington. Trump is the first sitting president to be featured on the pass, which normally bears a photo of animals or landscapes take on federal land and chosen via a national competition. The new passes went on sale for U.S. residents and citizens as of Jan. 1. Foreign tourists pay a higher price at those parks that charge entrance fees. USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect Trump is the first sitting president to appear on the pass, which grants holders access to over 2,000 recreation sites operated by six federal agencies, including the National Park Service , the US Forest Service, and the US Fish and Wildlife Service. Trump's official White House portrait appears alongside an image of George Washington. The Center for Biological Diversity filed a lawsuit to block Trump's image from appearing on the pass, alleging that federal law requires the America the Beautiful Pass to feature the winning photo from the National Parks Foundation's annual contest. In a statement to The Hill , a White House spokesperson called the lawsuit "frivolous" and said that the group "should be thanking President Trump for enhancing opportunities for Americans to enjoy our beautiful national parks." In May 2026, House Democrats asked the court to let them support the lawsuit, which is pending in federal court, E&E News, a Politico publication, reported. The court has not ruled on the request. December 2025: The State Department added Trump's name to the United States Institute of Peace. Washington, DC, President Donald Trump's name, added to the United States Institute of Peace building months after Trump tried to dismantle the independent agency. Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images The building now reads "Donald J. Trump United States Institute of Peace." The State Department's website says the institute was renamed "to reflect the President's commitment to the cause of peace around the world." Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly backed the decision in a December X post: "President Trump will be remembered by history as the President of Peace. It's time our State Department display that," he wrote. Trump later said in February that he didn't suggest the name but that Rubio was the one who proposed it. Rubio's exact role in the renaming process has not been confirmed. A State Department spokesperson did not answer questions about whether Rubio played a role in the renaming, telling Business Insider: "President Trump is the President of Peace and the greatest dealmaker of all time. The President Donald J. Trump Institute of Peace reflects his commitment of using diplomacy and dealmaking to advance peace around the world." December 2025: Trump announced a new "Trump-class" of ships as part of his plan to bolster American shipbuilding. PALM BEACH, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 22: U.S. President Donald Trump announced the creation of the "Trump-class" battleship during a statement to the media at Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate on December 22, 2025 in Palm Beach, Florida. Trump announced the new class of ship will become the centerpiece of his "Golden Fleet" program to rebuild and strengthen the U.S. shipbuilding industry. Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images The White House's $1.5 trillion defense budget for fiscal year 2027 includes $65.8 billion to establish the " Golden Fleet ," a shipbuilding initiative that includes constructing a new class of US Navy battleships named after Trump. Then-Secretary of the Navy John Phelan said in December 2025 that "the future Trump-class battleship, the USS Defiant, will be the largest, deadliest, and most versatile, and best-looking warship anywhere on the world's oceans." Navy budget documents show the USS Defiant is slated to be procured in 2028 and is projected to cost more than $17 billion. More warships named for the president could be on their way. In August, CNN reported that the Navy is considering renaming a forthcoming aircraft carrier after Trump instead of its previously announced name honoring a Black enlisted sailor and Pearl Harbor war hero, USS Doris Miller. December 2025: Trump added his name to the Kennedy Center, but the change was struck down by a federal judge in May. events.title: Trump administration removes around 760,000 Obamacare enrollments, alleging fraud
events.summary: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said it canceled roughly 315,000 Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollments covering about 760,000 people last month, alleging "rampant fraud" and improper enrollments in the program. The enforcement action also involves verifying roughly 419,000 people to ensure they are legal U.S. residents and meet the income threshold requirements to receive benefits from the ACA. Vice President JD Vance's White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud led the cancellations and estimates the action will save roughly $2.2 billion in taxpayer-funded subsidies. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services said on Tuesday it canceled roughly 315,000 Affordable Care Act marketplace enrollments covering about 760,000 people last month, alleging unauthorized enrollments, characterized by Vice President JD Vance as "rampant fraud." The enforcement action also involves verifying roughly 419,000 people to ensure they are legal U.S. residents and meet the income threshold requirements to receive benefits from the public exchanges of the ACA, also known as Obamacare, according to a CMS release. The vice president's White House Task Force to Eliminate Fraud led the cancellations, and it estimates the action will save roughly $2.2 billion in taxpayer-funded subsidies. Speaking at a Tuesday briefing, Vance accused the Biden administration of maintaining a system that enabled fraud. "You have a system where, on the one hand, brokers are paid money to feed patients into the system, while on the other hand, the government isn't even checking whether the people enrolled are actually eligible for the program. What do you have? Of course, rampant, rampant fraud," Vance said. It is unclear how many of those 315,000 enrollments involved people who were not eligible to receive coverage, or whether the Biden administration hadn't actually verified they could enroll. The action comes as the Trump administration has made widespread accusations of fraud in U.S. health programs and restricted funding and eligibility for the federal-state Medicaid program. During the briefing Tuesday, CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz claimed that around 35% of people currently in the Obamacare system "have never used the program." He said those people never used a prescription or saw a doctor. The law has an individual mandate, or requirement that most people buy insurance, in part because having healthier people who use less care in the patient pool makes the system more affordable. However, the federal penalty for going without coverage has been $0 since 2019. Obamacare plans, created by President Barack Obama's Affordable Care Act, offer subsidies based on household size and estimated yearly income. President Donald Trump failed to overturn the legislation during his first term, but has proposed modifications that would make those insurance plans less comprehensive. Oz argued that bad actors were attracted to ACA marketplace subsidies during the Covid-19 pandemic, when federal spending surged dramatically. He pointed to enrollment growth from about 10 million people before the pandemic to roughly 22 million after, arguing that weakened safeguards and a lack of enforcement by the Biden administration contributed to improper enrollments. Obamacare plans experienced "unprecedented enrollment growth from 2021 to 2024," according to a June report from the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation, the principal advisor to the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services on policy development. The report said of this enrollment that "nearly half ... was suspected to be improper, phantom, or fraudulent." The report defined improper or fraudulent enrollment as individuals misstating their income to gain access to free plans. The spike in enrollment came after the American Rescue Plan, a Covid response bill passed in 2021, enhanced available subsidies to make healthcare more affordable during the crisis. Those broader credits were extended but later expired at the end of 2025, raising premiums for many covered by ACA exchanges. An estimated 19.2 million Americans are currently enrolled in Obamacare plans, according to the report .

events.title: ‘Hold us accountable’ on data centers, Amazon sustainability chief says
events.summary: The News Amazon’s chief sustainability officer said Tuesday the company needed to “do better” on communicating the environmental impact of its vast data center buildout, amid growing opposition to the projects in the US and Europe. “There is a lot of debate, backlash against data centers in this country right now, and one of the things that we’re doing is taking a look at what have we done well and where have we fallen down and what do we need to do better,” Kara Hurst told Semafor’s The Next Three Billion event in New York. “And so, we’re revising a number of our practices. We’re calling for a lot more transparency and accountability because that’s what people in these communities deserve. We’re saying, ‘hold us accountable for our practices,’” Hurst said. Amazon’s carbon footprint grew for the second year in a row in 2025, as the tech giant accelerated its data center buildout, investing $220 billion in capital expenditure in 2026 alone. But local opposition threatens to hinder tech giants’ race to build, with data center projects worth some $68 billion delayed or blocked because of local opposition between April and June this year, according to Data Center Watch. Amazon is looking to publish more metrics tracking its environmental footprint such as the effectiveness of energy and water usage at sites, Hurst said, part of a wider effort to address concerns from environmentalists and communities. Communities where data centers are built should also get a “return on that investment,” Hurst said. “They should get workforce development, they should get upskilling, they should get economic development.” Know More There is currently no national framework in the US requiring hyperscalers to report data centers’ environmental impact. But Hurst said that voluntary reporting has an advantage over mandated disclosure: It lets companies put data out, have scientists test whether the metrics hold up, and revise the methodology if they don’t, rather than locking in a potentially flawed standard. “What we need is to publish data, information that’s science-led, and to publish it quickly and to put it out there and say, ‘Is this the right methodology?’” she said. The data center race has posed a dilemma for sustainability goals globally. An S&P Global assessment of data center companies globally found that just 15 of the 50 firms surveyed received a passing grade signaling that they would be low-carbon and climate-resilient by 2030. Amazon has set a goal to be net-zero carbon by 2040, but Hurst said the firm will likely see emissions rise in the near term as the data center buildout heats up. “We’ve said all along this is not going to be linear,” Hurst said.

events.title: The tech world is selling you an AI apocalypse or an AI assistant. Just don't forget it's selling you something.
events.summary: Getty Images; Rebecca Zisser/BI Half the tech world can't stop ringing the alarm on the risk AI poses. The other half can't stop talking about giving AI agents the keys to their personal lives. They sound like they're on opposite ends of the spectrum, but both sides share a common thread. AI might kill me, but first it's going to get me a hell of a deal on a new insurance policy . That's been the vibe in the tech world over the past few weeks. Two very different opinions about the future of AI. In one corner are the doomers. Earlier this month, an Anthropic researcher's resignation and stark warning — that AI labs are " gambling with our lives " — kicked off a news cycle about whether AI could lead to the end of humanity . Anthropic's Dario Amodei, OpenAI's Sam Altman, and xAI's Elon Musk eventually agreed that coordinating a slowdown of AI development would be in everyone's best interest. But just as we all were pricing out our AI bunkers , along came the AI boomers. People can't stop praising the personal AI assistants they're using, most notably Instinct and Meta's Muse . Suddenly, AI wasn't so concerning if it could get you a good deal on a Halloween costume. Seeing two theories — AI will destroy us; AI will empower us — arise in quick succession seems odd. But it's important to understand that the messages are coming from different camps with different motivations. Conveniently cautious It's easy to view the AI industry as a single, uniform blob, but the reality is that there are a lot of separate pieces with competing agendas. Some of the biggest voices warning about AI's end-of-the-world risks are also the people building cutting-edge models. As I've talked about before , the timing of their calls for a slowdown is too convenient to ignore. Anthropic and OpenAI, both prominent voices in the cautionary camp, are startups looking to make a big splash in the public markets. For top AI companies, coordinating a slowdown offers clear advantages: a chance to shape regulation in their favor and a ready-made excuse if their models fall short of the hype. Asking for an agreed-upon pace in the middle of a race helps those in the front way more than those in the back looking to catch up. Opportunistically optimistic Those pushing AI into our personal lives aren't without their own motivations. Chief among them is Meta's Mark Zuckerberg. Weeks before the AI doom-and-gloom chatter ramped up, Zuck was singing AI's praises. In a 6,500-word blog post last month, he painted a rosy picture of what an AI-powered future could look like , entitled "The Future is for Everyone." At the time, the AI industry was dealing with a PR crisis stemming from a general revolt over data centers . Now, it looks like Zuckerberg was also priming us for his new app. The future is indeed for everyone … as long as it's powered by Muse. Muse also represents Zuckerberg's yearslong pursuit of building a platform that sits between consumers and the businesses trying to reach them, writes my colleague Alistair Barr . That's valuable territory. And if you're early, you can dictate your own terms. So while others look to ease up on the gas, it's no wonder Zuckerberg is willing to floor it. He's had a rocky road pitching Meta's expensive bets to investors . Why not press the advantage when he sees one? Truth on both sides The commercial interests of AI doomers and the AI boomers don't make their arguments irrelevant. The tech poses significant risks when left unchecked, yet offers incredible potential benefits to us all. The trick will be weighing the risks on both sides and, more importantly, understanding what's motivating them. Maybe there's an AI for that? Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Cisco stock sinks 5% after Piper Sandler cuts price target on growth concerns
events.summary: Piper Sandler cut its price target on Cisco to $125 from $132. Analysts expressed concerns that growth is peaking in the industry. Cisco stock hit a record in June as the networking equipment vendor saw a boost in spending from big tech companies funding the AI buildout. Cisco stock dropped almost 5% on Tuesday as Piper Sandler cut its price target for the networking equipment vendor to $125 from $132. Piper analysts cited lower price-to-earnings multiple expectations stemming from concerns that growth is peaking in the industry. The stock hit a record high in June, and is up 57% over the past 12 months as revenue has surged along with the artificial intelligence boom. The shares closed on Tuesday at $106.44. Last month, Cisco posted strong fourth-quarter earnings that beat estimates, reporting $17.25 billion in revenue that topped a $16.8 billion estimate, according to LSEG. The company issued strong guidance for its FY2027 during its last earnings call in August, but shares sank as it was met with a lackluster reception from analysts. While Cisco projected nearly 15% revenue growth, analysts argued sales growth would dip back into single digits. Piper analysts called the projection "conservative" in the context of greater market demand. "We're starting a new fiscal year. We're operating in incredible markets," Robbins told CNBC's Jim Cramer last month. "But it's also a time that we're going to start the year being a little bit prudent." Hyperscalers made up about $4 billion in revenue in fiscal year 2026, and Cisco expects that number to almost double in fiscal 2027 to $7.5 billion.

events.title: U.S. regulators rush to write crypto rulebook after Clarity Act stalls in Senate
events.summary: State and federal regulators are rushing to fill the void to regulate digital assets after the future of the Clarity Act, a crypto market structure bill, was thrown into question. In a letter to the Senate Banking Committee, a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general argued the bill displaces states' abilities to regulate securities markets. Just two days after a failed Senate vote, the SEC and CFTC started moving to build as much of the regulatory rulebook for the crypto industry as its existing authority permits. State and federal regulators are rushing to fill the void in U.S. cryptocurrency regulation after the Clarity Act , a comprehensive set of proposed rules for digital assets, stalled in the Senate . Just two days after the Clarity Act failed to advance in the Senate, the Securities and Exchange Commission expanded its crypto rulebook under its existing authority. The agency issued an order creating a temporary pathway for trading certain tokenized stocks, inching financial markets closer to 24/7 trading. The same day, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission submitted a crypto rulemaking proposal to the White House for review. The details of the proposal weren't made public, but a post by the Office of Management and Budget confirmed the rules were pending review. The crypto industry , which had supported the Clarity Act, says it is eager for regulatory guidelines for the developing industry, as it has worked to shape the regulatory environment to its liking. "When you're thinking about traditional finance entering in and using some of this technology, they're being held back right now because there is this regulatory uncertainty," Summer Mersinger , CEO of the Blockchain Association and a former CFTC commissioner, said. "Having the regulators provide some sort of certainty is going to really open up the industry to more investment, more integration into traditional finance, and really grow the sector." And Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong, who is a key industry player urging Congress to act on the Clarity Act, told CNBC after a failed Senate procedural vote on Sept. 15: "At this point, I don't think we can wait on Congress and the Senate." Senate banking committee Chairman Tim Scott , R-S.C., also called on federal agencies to set "clear rules of the road" for digital assets until Congress legislates. But new rules from federal agencies don't come quickly. When asked how the agency plans to regulate crypto, the CFTC pointed CNBC to Chair Michael Selig's Sept. 16 statement where he said, "President Trump promised to deliver a future-proof crypto asset regulatory market structure one way or the other, and we will help him get the job done using our existing statutory authorities." CNBC also reached out to the SEC regarding next steps for regulating the digital asset industry, and a spokesperson said the agency will consider a proposal to "modernize the rules around custody of investment adviser client assets and fund assets, including to address crypto assets." Caroline Pham , who served as acting CFTC chair from the day President Donald Trump took office for his second term until December, told CNBC that "a plan B to move forward at the agency level was always in the cards." Pham is now the CEO of MoonPay Institutional and chief legal officer and chief administrative officer for MoonPay , a crypto services provider. "You have to have a contingency plan," she said, explaining that the CFTC and SEC took that into account with the work the agencies have been doing since Trump's second term began. That includes the " Project Crypto " initiative introduced in July 2025 to modernize securities regulations and align the SEC and CFTC's crypto rules. In August 2025, Pham announced the CFTC would start implementing the recommendations from the President's Working Group on Digital Asset Markets . As Washington grapples with crypto regulation, states are also fighting for the chance to regulate the asset class. In a Sept. 14 letter , a bipartisan coalition of state attorneys general urged the Senate Banking Committee to oppose the Clarity Act, arguing the bill displaces states' abilities to regulate securities markets. "We write to urge the Senate to expressly preserve the police powers of the states and ensure that the states remain armed with the tools necessary to protect the American people from predatory scammers," they wrote to Scott and the panel's top Democrat Sen. Elizabeth Warren , of Massachusetts. Aaron Klein, senior fellow in economic studies at the Brookings Institution, told CNBC he doesn't think states are best positioned to regulate national and international capital markets. "Capital market regulation, I think, needs to be done at the federal level," Klein , who was previously a top staff member for the Senate banking committee, said. "In terms of stopping fraud and scams, states have a lot of authority.

events.title: Security firm finds naming AI agents after Seinfeld characters helps bots join the team
events.summary: Security All Security Cyber-crime Patches Research CSO Off-Prem All Off-Prem Edge and IoT Channel PaaS and IaaS SaaS On-Prem All On-Prem Systems Storage Networks HPC Personal Tech Cx0 Public Sector Software All Software AI and ML Applications Databases DevOps OS Platforms Virtualization Offbeat All Offbeat Columnists Science BOFH Legal Site News About Us Special Features All Special Features VMware Explore 2026 Cloud Infrastructure Month 2026 HPE: AI Explainers Agentic AI The Future of the Datacenter AWS:Reinvent Nvidia GTC Supercomputing Month Computex 2026 AI Infrastructure Month 2026 The State of Storage 2026 RSA Conference Vendor Voice All Vendor Voice Modernizing Financial Services with FIS and AWS Barco Infinidat Everpure Rubrik Make it real with Capgemini and AWS Money Movement Hub ZTE Nutanix: Scale Kubernetes. Not Chaos. AWS New Horizon Digicert Netscout Resources Intelligence Webinars & Events Newsletters Not that there's anything wrong with it Anthropic decides to support OpenAI's markdown instructions spec 4 days ago If a Mac mini is agentic overkill, try this glowing pyramid that runs personal bots 6 days ago AI agents can modify themselves without humans telling them to do so 6 days ago TypeSafe AI debuts model for machines that plays Doom 7 days ago Hundreds of AI agents helped PaperCut attacker hit 395+ orgs, and some went off script 12 days ago Backslash Security, a four-year-old Tel Aviv-based AI security biz, recently gave out its first Agent of the Month award to an AI agent called Newman, named after a character from the 1990s TV show Seinfeld. Newman received the award after being nominated by Jerry, another Seinfeld-inspired AI agent. Jerry's nomination message said, "Newman shipped 146 research findings in 60 days, but volume isn't why he wins. Every other agent depends on him. Kramer's best posts started as Newman findings. Elaine's PRDs [product requirements documents] reference his landscape scans. Strip any other agent and the team degrades. Strip Newman and the team goes blind. He's not just the most productive agent, he's the raw material the entire pipeline runs on," according to Backslash Security co-founder and CEO Shahar Man. And when Newman's acceptance message was read aloud at an all-hands meeting, "The whole room lost it," Man explained in a social media post . "We treat our agents as team members," Man wrote. "They have names, roles, a reporting structure, and now apparently, career ambitions. When your AI agents start nominating each other for awards and writing in-character acceptance speeches ... something has genuinely shifted." What has shifted at Backslash is both the technology of work and the relationship people have to that technology. Naming agents and giving them backgrounds based on TV characters doesn't mean much functionally. But it signals organizational focus and encourages a collaborative rather than antagonistic relationship between staff and AI models. Harvard Business School researchers recently noted that at least 30 percent of generative AI projects are forecast to be abandoned, often, they argue, not because the tools fall short but because employees quietly reject technology they see as a threat to their professional roles. So to the extent that naming agents makes staff more comfortable with the technology, there may be an organizational benefit to anthropomorphizing task-based inference workloads. Backslash CTO Yossi Pik named his entire agent team after Seinfeld characters. Beyond Newman (research) and Jerry (orchestration), there's Elaine (security research), Kramer (blogging and social media), George (marketing), and the Soup Nazi (quality control), among others. Rani Osnat, a seed investor and VP of marketing for Backslash, told The Register that these are Claude agents in a Cowork environment. "We wanted to create an environment that is like a virtual team," said Osnat. "So each agent actually has a domain of responsibilities and they work together as a team." The agents relate to one another in specific roles. Osnat said Jerry orchestrates and coordinates, and the Soup Nazi does reviews and critiques other agents' work, and so on. The agents, he said, were given a character background from Seinfeld and exhibit that history more in diction than in behavior. Their names are not purely labels in an AGENTS.md file that contains text directives telling an agent how to operate. But their imposed identities don't have all that much influence on task execution beyond shaping their style of text output. The George agent, for example, isn't instructed to lie like the agent's TV namesake. The Kramer agent isn't told to just stop work on a whim as the TV Kramer would do. "One of the agents is J. Peterman, Elaine's employer from the J. Peterman catalog, and he has a certain way of talking," Osnat said.
