events.title: Trump says he would back ban on diesel exports
events.summary: US President Donald Trump has said he would back proposals to halt American diesel exports in a bid to ease prices for drivers at the pumps. His comments come after Republicans lawmakers put pressure on the president ahead of November's mid-term elections to curb exports, as diesel prices soar to record highs in the US. Speaking on the sidelines at the United Nations General Assembly, Trump suggested keeping domestic supplies inside the US could also ease broader petrol prices. "I've called for that too. I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel. That could have a little bit of an effect on regular automobile gasoline," he said . US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confirmed officials were assessing "whether a full or partial ban would work" without disrupting refinery capabilities. National average diesel prices surpassed $6.50 (£4.87) a gallon on Tuesday according to American Automobile Association data, a new high. The conflict in the Middle East has constrained global oil supplies, putting pressure on pump prices. The surge in the cost of diesel has sparked political urgency ahead of crucial mid-term elections on 3 November, with several Republicans pressing the administration to restrict the fuel's export to ease financial strain on voters. US Representative Ashley Hinson, a Republican running for Senate in Iowa, said on Monday that the state's consumers were "being squeezed and shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump." In Alaska on Tuesday, Senator Dan Sullivan similarly urged for a "temporary pause of American diesel and exports" to rebuild domestic reserves. Adding to the global market volatility, Ukraine's targeting of Russian energy facilities has knocked out the country's refining capacity. "It is a serious hit on the Russians," Trump said during a meeting with Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelensky on Tuesday. "It's also a serious hit on the price of diesel." Trump confirmed he would discuss the strikes with the Ukrainian president, alongside broader efforts to negotiate an end to the conflict. "I think it's going to happen," he said. Kyiv has intensified drone attacks on Russian processing plants in recent months to choke off the Kremlin's primary source of war funding. Because Russia ranks among the world's leading diesel suppliers, reduced refining capacity – combined with Moscow's own strict export bans – has severely squeezed global reserves. While restricting US exports could offer short-term relief for American drivers, a ban may risk pushing up prices internationally. The US exports roughly 1.3 million barrels of diesel per day – nearly a quarter of its refining output. Cutting these shipments could put pressure on supplies for Western allies, including the UK and the Netherlands, which have relied on American fuel to cover deficits left by sanctions on Russian energy. events.title: British backpacker left alone at night by Greyhound bus in outback
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts British backpacker left by Greyhound bus at South Australian roadhouse alone at night British backpacker Emma, pictured during a separate trip, was left at a toilet stop in South Australia's Far North. ( Supplied ) A British woman was left in an small outback community after dark when her Greyhound bus drove off following a toilet stop. The traveller says she waited for almost three hours before police eventually picked her up. Greyhound says its investigation into the circumstances is ongoing. A British backpacker has been left stranded at an outback toilet block in the middle of the night after her interstate coach service departed without her. Emma had been travelling in Australia since late August, and on September 5 she boarded a Greyhound bus at Alice Springs, heading towards Adelaide. She said the bus made a scheduled stop at Pimba at about midnight, and the driver extended the stop to 25 minutes after the onboard bathroom malfunctioned. "[The driver] said he's going to ... add an extra five minutes onto what would have been a 20-minute stop at Pimba," Emma said. "There's a queue to get into the loos, of course, so I queue, and I wait, and then I get in there, use the loo, brush my teeth." Emma said about 15 minutes had passed from when the bus pulled in to when she exited the toilet , leaving her about 10 minutes to return to her seat. "I leave and the bus isn't there," she said. British backpackers are coming to Australia in record numbers, but the traditional working holiday has changed. Emma said she was left alone at the truck stop toilets, near a service station that was shut at that time of night, in a remote area surrounded by desert and scrub. "It was four degrees [Celsius] that night, I found out later," Emma said. "I had my little rucksack, a little bit of water, no food, didn't have my passport, didn't have anything. Most of my stuff was still on the bus "So at that point I start sort of worrying a bit more. I call Greyhound. They don't answer." Emma said she rang Triple Zero (000) for help. Eventually a police vehicle carrying out a custody transfer from Roxby Downs to Port Augusta picked her up at about 2:30am. "It was so nice to be warm and safe, because by 2:30, I'd been out there for nearly three hours," she said. "I'm standing in the toilet block because it's slightly sheltered and therefore about a couple of degrees warmer than the rest of the place." Greyhound Australia has confirmed the passenger did not return to its bus in Pimba. ( Supplied ) The tourist collected most of her belongings, except for one bag, at Port Augusta after local police liaised with Greyhound. She then booked a regional bus through a different company to get to Adelaide. "I went to considerable extra expense because I had to buy a hotel and breakfast and food, and another bus to Adelaide because they [Greyhound] didn't take me to Adelaide the way they were supposed to," she said. "I'd probably want my ticket back and a bit of compensation as well because you don't endanger your passengers like that." Do you know more about this story? Get in touch with Matthew Ward Agius: agius.matthew[at]abc.net.au Emma's backpack was meant to be left for collection at Adelaide's Central Bus Station; however, she said the bag was dropped off at another location outside of the CBD. "Then started a lovely five-hour adventure trying to extract it [the backpack] from them," she said. Emma told ABC News that she made a complaint to Greyhound Australia following the incident. She received an emailed response from the company on Tuesday evening but said that email did not explain why she was left behind. "They’ve made an offer [of compensation], which is surprising given that they say that their review is still ongoing," she said. In a statement, Greyhound Australia said its investigation into the incident was ongoing, but confirmed a passenger "did not return to the coach following a scheduled comfort stop at Pimba". After receiving notification of the incident, Greyhound Australia said it "worked with police to locate the passenger and assist them to a place of safety". The company said it provided "24/7 customer support" through 1300 GREYHOUND with "an out-of-hours emergency service available" for urgent travel-related matters. It said customers could also reach out on the Greyhound website and its online chatbot. "We have not identified any issues indicating the emergency service was unavailable during the period in question," the spokesperson said. "The safety and wellbeing of our passengers remains our highest priority.

events.title: Nasdaq reaches record high close, AI stocks rally
events.summary: Traders working on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange, in New York City, on Sept 16. The Nasdaq hit a record high, driven by AI-related stocks like Micron Technology, while the S&P 500 stayed just below its record amid stable oil prices around US$100 per barrel. Meta Platforms’ AI assistant, Muse, boosted chip stocks but raised concerns about competition with retailers and consumer companies, causing some tech stocks to decline. Investors awaited the US-China summit for potential trade and AI regulation talks, while the Fed maintained a cautious stance on interest rates amid inflation risks and market support. NEW YORK - The Nasdaq notched a record high close on Sept 22, lifted by Micron Technology and other AI-related stocks, while the S&P 500 hovered just below a record high as oil prices traded around US$100 per barrel. Chip stocks added to recent gains while consumer-related software shares lost ground. Investors focused on the strong reception of Meta Platforms’ AI assistant, which launched this month and can send emails and complete transactions on behalf of a user. The success of the AI assistant, called Muse, has fuelled gains for AI-related chip stocks in recent days. Yet, some worried it could compete with retailers, online brokerages and other consumer companies. Amazon on Sept 21 blocked the agent from shopping on its platform. “There are a lot of tech stocks that are down today on Muse-related fears of one sort or another,” said Jed Ellerbroek, portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management. “People fear that Muse will be used to manage your insurance relationships, book your travel and search for stuff to buy.” Ride-hailing apps Uber Technologies and Lyft lost ground, while Expedia and Charles Schwab also fell. Memory chipmakers Micron and SanDisk both rallied. Oil prices were choppy near US$100 a barrel, while the yield on the benchmark 10-year Treasury note hovered around 4.94 per cent after US President Donald Trump warned in a speech to the UN General Assembly that he could “annihilate the Islamic Republic” if no deal is reached to end the Middle East conflict. Investors also awaited a US-China summit on Sept 23, with traders speculating the trade truce with Beijing could be extended and talks could touch on AI regulation. “What people are looking for is at least the start of a conversation that maybe you can come up with some sort of global framework as opposed to fighting each other and having this race and so,” said Joe Saluzzi, head of equity market structure research at Themis Trading. According to preliminary data, the S&P 500 lost 0.43 points, or 0.01 per cent, to end at 7,764.27 points, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 121.15 points, or 0.45 per cent, to 27,243.24. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 184.94 points, or 0.36 per cent, to 51,863.89. The S&P 500 was less than 1 per cent below its Aug 13 record high close. Even as it trades near record highs, the S&P 500 is valued at just under 19 times expected earnings, its lowest valuation since 2023, according to LSEG data. AI-related heavyweights are responsible for much of the recent increase in earnings expectations. JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo both lost ground. Boston Federal Reserve President Susan Collins wrote she supported last week’s interest rate increase, citing inflation risks. New York Fed President John Williams said the Fed’s framework for controlling short-term rates has been effective in supporting financial markets. Traders see a 53 per cent chance the Fed will increase interest rates by at least 25 basis points in October, the CME Group’s FedWatch Tool showed. REUTERS

events.title: Central Victorian council votes to keep divisive public holiday
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Bendigo keeps public holiday for local horse race, despite push from businesses Bendigo Cup Day will continue to be a public holiday. ( Supplied: Bendigo Jockey Club ) Bendigo will retain a public holiday for Bendigo Cup Day after council voted on Monday to keep the date following community consultation. A small margin of community respondents voted to keep the date, while a majority of businesses wanted a change, citing operational concerns. The council will apply to the state government, which makes the final decision on local public holiday arrangements. A Central Victorian council has been drawn into a local public holiday debate, backing a slim majority of locals who wanted to keep a controversial race-day holiday. The City of Greater Bendigo council voted on Monday night to keep Bendigo Cup Day as the local public holiday for another five years. The 4-1 vote to retain the current arrangement will see part of the shire taking a public holiday on Wednesday, October 28, a week prior to the Melbourne Cup. Residents in the municipality east of the Campaspe River, including Heathcote, will continue to observe Melbourne Cup as its public holiday. The decision followed a community survey that drew 2,672 responses, with mayor Thomas Prince calling it the council's "third most ever engaged survey". The meeting saw councillors vote in line with the slim majority of respondents. About 38 per cent of survey respondents said they wanted to keep Bendigo Cup Day holiday, while 36.5 per cent preferred Melbourne Cup Day and 24.7 per cent preferred the Friday of the Bendigo Show. Meanwhile, just over half of businesses surveyed, making up 4 per cent of the responses, called for the date to be changed to Melbourne Cup Day, citing business operation concerns and alignment with the rest of the state as reasons to switch. Thomas Prince says he was "challenged" by the survey. ( Supplied: City of Greater Bendigo ) The mayor told the meeting he was "challenged" by the survey. "It feels like a popularity contest around what the community want," Cr Prince said. "Most of our contributors, I think, will be related to the sports racing industry and the jockey club and those at the Bendigo Show, and they're very self-invested ideas and opinions. "The question is, 'What is most important for Bendigo?' "What's best for Bendigo … is that we want our own holiday. We want a chance to celebrate who we are." Eppalock Ward councillor Aaron Spong was the only councillor to vote against the motion, arguing the business feedback deserved more weight. "Tradition does matter, but so does practicality," Cr Spong said. Epsom Ward councillor Andrea Metcalf, who moved the motion, said analysis by consulting firm IER and council data put the 2025 Bendigo Cup's local economic activity at between $2.9 million and $3.2 million, with more than 6,500 people attending the cup. The Bendigo Show draws about 20,000 people across its two days, five days before the cup. "Both the show and the cup can be successful under the current arrangement," Cr Metcalf said. Cr Prince told ABC Central Victoria Breakfast the alternative of moving the holiday to Show Day would have come at the Bendigo Cup's expense. "To elevate that to probably potentially completely squash the Bendigo Cup day also just didn't make sense," he said. The Bendigo Jockey Club welcomed the vote, with chief executive Paul Scullie saying the club had heard "the importance of ensuring our business community benefits from the public holiday" and wanted racegoers to "shop locally, stay locally, eat and drink locally". The council will now apply to the state government, which makes the final decision on local public holiday arrangements.

events.title: I'm a personal stylist for corporate clients. There are 5 mistakes I always tell them to avoid when dressing for work.
events.summary: As a personal stylist, I've noticed several mistakes corporate professionals make when getting dressed for work. Jason Jean/WWD via Getty Images; Alyssa Powell/BI I'm a personal stylist who helps corporate clients build a polished, authentic office wardrobe . To spice up an all-black outfit, I recommend professionals add a textured heel or loafer. Instead of avoiding accessories, adding a statement belt or stud earrings can elevate a simple look. As a personal stylist for corporate clients, I believe that picking out an outfit shouldn't be the hardest part of someone's morning — it should be the easiest. After four years of helping professionals build wardrobes that suit their lifestyles and boost their confidence in the office, I've learned what works — and what doesn't — when dressing for the workplace. These are five of the most common mistakes I always tell clients to avoid. Relying on an all-black outfit eliminates any personality. Ranta Images/iStock One of the biggest mistakes I see people make is what I call the "all-black blob." Because wearing black feels easy, professional, and safe, people tend to use this same formula every day: a black ballet flat , black straight-leg trousers, a black tee, and a black blazer. There's nothing necessarily wrong with that attire, but when everything is the same, I think it starts to eliminate any sense of personality or interest in the outfit. Instead, I recommend mixing in one unique item. Streetstyleshooters/Getty Images I think adding one unique item — like mixing cotton with wool, cashmere, leather, or suede — to an all-black outfit adds more dimension to the look. That way, even though everything is black, the outfit doesn't feel flat. Another way to elevate an all-black look is to incorporate an interesting pair of shoes. I love snakeskin as a way to add a little pattern to an otherwise simple ensemble. I also recommend trying a loafer in a deep brown or navy, or grabbing a suede pair to add even more texture. The same goes for shirts and ties. I wouldn't necessarily wear a black button-down with a black blazer . Instead, I recommend breaking it up with a different color, texture, or accessory. Wearing a suit isn't the only way to look professional. Astrakan Images/Getty Images Of course, if someone's job or corporate event requires a suit, then they should absolutely wear one. But in any other case, looking professional doesn't always mean reaching for a blazer. I love the look of a lady jacket or shorter dress shirt instead. Edward Berthelot/Getty Images Rather than wearing a suit, I recommend that women look for a lady jacket — a collarless outerwear that hits nicely at the waist — which gives a more relaxed feel while still looking polished. For men, I suggest classic trousers paired with a shorter dress shirt that can be worn untucked. Skipping accessories leaves outfits feeling unfinished. Jeremy Moeller/Getty Images I find that a lot of clients tend to stay away from accessorizing at work. However, embellishments to an outfit don't have to be loud to make an impact. Just a few pieces of dainty jewelry can make a huge difference. Wirestock/iStock Something as simple as a few dainty layered necklaces, small studs, a great ring, or a delicate bracelet can add interest to otherwise simple work attire . And if a workplace allows for a little more fun, I recommend wearing a statement earring, necklace, or belt to bring even more personality to the look. Thinking that a work bag can't be both chic and practical is a big mistake. KoldoyChris/Getty Images A work bag absolutely needs to be functional, as it carries a myriad of things, such as a laptop, folders, a water bottle, lunch, and maybe even an extra pair of shoes. However, that doesn't mean it needs to be boring. People sometimes assume that if a bag is practical, it can't also be chic, but I don't think that's true. Bags with textured leather or hardware instantly elevate a corporate look. Edward Berthelot/Getty Images I've found many bags that not only provide space and functionality, but also look more elevated and make a statement — specifically those with hardware elements, textured leather, or pebbled finishes. There's no need to have separate work and personal-life wardrobes. Christian Vierig/Getty Images I hear this all the time: "Well, it's just for work. I'd rather spend my money on the clothes I wear in my actual life." However, the reality is that if someone is going into an office five days a week, their work clothes are a huge part of their actual life. So if someone spends hours and hours in these clothes every single week, why wouldn't they invest in them? People should look through their own closets before buying any more work clothes. Tatiana Meteleva/Getty Images Investing doesn't just mean buying something expensive. It means selecting breathable fabrics, choosing pieces that feel good against the skin, and paying attention to clothes that actually make sense for the season. Before purchasing a whole new wardrobe for the office, I always recommend clients look through their own closets first. Many work-appropriate pieces can also transition outside the 9-to-5, including heels, ballet flats, and bags. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The 21 best state universities in the US, ranked
events.summary: UCLA is tied for first this year for best state schools. Mario Tama/Getty Images US News & World Report ranks the best universities across the US every year. While many of the top schools are private, every state in the union has its own public system. We used US News' 2027 ranking to compile a list of the 21 top public schools. This back-to-school season, the cost and value of higher education are top of mind. In a time when going to college can put you in hundreds of thousands of dollars in debt , and as more tech moguls share that they skipped university altogether, it could be worth considering a public school. Every state has some sort of public school system, though they're not all created equal. Just as private schools have  the Ivy League , some state schools stand above the rest —  Forbes now releases  its own list of "Public Ivies" each year. Public schools are also generally cheaper than private schools, especially if you stay in-state. But even paying out-of-state tuition at some public schools can cost half as much as the most expensive colleges charge. We used US News & World Report's 2027 ranking of best national universities to identify the top 21 public schools in the country. The list does not include liberal arts colleges focused on undergraduate education or regional universities with limited doctoral programs, although those are typically private schools. Its ranking evaluated over 400 US colleges across multiple metrics, including graduation rates, debt loads, average salaries, and admissions rates, among others, using data reported by schools and third-party sources . For its 2027 list, US News introduced a new "earnings by major" metric. College rankings have faced scrutiny over the years, with critics of US News & World Report's lists arguing that they can pressure schools to perform well on certain metrics to boost their standing. Skeptics have also questioned the ranking methodology, saying it may fail to capture key, less quantifiable factors that add to a school's quality. US News has defended the rankings as a helpful resource, while admitting comparing colleges "can be challenging," and the lists "don't capture every nuance." "But we reject our critics' paternalistic view that students are somehow incapable of discerning for themselves from this information which school is the best fit," US News & World Report executive chairman and CEO Eric Gertler wrote in 2023 for the Wall Street Journal . Here are the 21 highest-ranked public universities in the US, according to US News & World Report's 2027 rankings. 19 (tie). College of William & Mary The sign for William and Mary college outside the campus in downtown Williamsburg. Eli Wilson/iStock National ranking: #52 (tie) The first school on this list (but not the last) located in Virginia is the College of William & Mary, which is in Williamsburg. It's named for King William III and Queen Mary II, who ruled England from 1689 to 1702. The college itself was founded in 1693, making it the second- oldest college in the US . About 7,000 undergraduates are enrolled. It ranked highly for its commitment to teaching undergrads rather than focusing on graduate-level research. 19 (tie). University of Georgia The Arch and entrance to the University of Georgia's North Campus JENNIFER E. WOLF/iStock National ranking: #52 (tie) UGA, located in Athens, was chartered by the state in 1785, making it the oldest state-chartered university in the US. It has an enrollment of about 32,000 undergraduate students. Per US News, UGA has the No. 2 insurance program in the country, which was founded in 1965. 19 (tie). Virginia Tech April 18, 2018: Historic Virginia Tech Polytechnic Institute and State University College campus with Burruss hall facade exterior in spring, krblokhin/iStock National ranking: #52 (tie) The town of Blacksburg is home to Virginia Tech, or the Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University, founded in 1872. Virginia Tech has about 31,000 undergraduate students enrolled. It ranks No. 6 for the best industrial/manufacturing engineering program. 17 (tie). University of Washington A scenic view of the University of Washington campus before a college basketball game between the Washington Huskies and the Minnesota Golden Gophers at the Alaska Airlines Arena at Hec Edmundson Pavilion on February 14, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. Mitchell Layton/Getty Images National ranking: #49 (tie) Founded in 1861, the University of Washington is located in the middle of Seattle and has an undergraduate enrollment of about 41,000 students. UW has strong nursing (tied for No. 1) and computer science programs (tied for No. 8). 17 (tie). University of Maryland, College Park College Park, Maryland October 27, 2024: Entrance Welcome sign at the University of Maryland College Park, Maryland Campus arlutz73/iStock National ranking: #49 (tie) The College Park campus is the largest in the UMD system, with about 31,000 undergraduate students. It was founded in 1856. College Park is just over 8 miles from downtown Washington, DC, and 30 miles from Baltimore, making it a relatively easy commute to either city. UMD's cybersecurity program ranks at No. 8. 14 (tie). University of California, Santa Barbara Architecture at the University of California, Santa Barbara campus in Santa Barbara, California taken on June 17, 2025. Kevin Koeppen Photography/iStock National ranking: #44 Nearly 24,000 undergraduates call UCSB, founded in 1909, home. Much can be said about UCSB's strong academics, but it's probably most famous for its proximity to the beach, making it a dream school for aspiring surfers everywhere. 14 (tie). Rutgers University — New Brunswick Rutgers University Welcome Sign at the College Avenue Campus in New Brunswick, NJ Hal Goodtree/iStock National ranking: #44 (tie) Rutgers has three campuses across New Jersey, but the biggest, located in New Brunswick, was ruled its best. It was founded in 1766 as Queen's College, before getting renamed Rutgers in 1825. Approximately 38,000 undergraduates are enrolled at the New Brunswick campus. 14 (tie). The Ohio State University Aerial view of Columbus Ohio stock photo espiegle/Getty Images/iStockphoto National ranking: #44 The Ohio State University, or OSU, has an undergraduate enrollment of about 47,000 students. Founded in 1870, it's located north of downtown Columbus, the Buckeye State's capital. OSU has a well-regarded nursing program (No. 4), accounting program (No. 12), and supply chain/logistics program (No. 5). 8 (tie). University of Wisconsin — Madison Bascom Hall located on the University of Wisconsin, Madison campus in Madison Wisconsin framed by tree and banner. Kevin Koeppen Photography/iStock National ranking: #34 (tie) UW-Madison's 939-acre campus, located in the heart of Madison, is home to 39,000 undergraduate students. events.title: Trump TV is live. Here's what it's actually showing
events.summary: As President Trump fights the press over coverage, the White House launched its own 24/7 streaming channel — Trump TV. Why it matters: Trump TV gives the president a White House-run video platform to reach the public without relying on traditional news organizations. So far, Trump TV resembles a round-the-clock presidential highlight reel more than a news network. Driving the news: Trump TV launched the same day major TV networks suspended White House pool coverage — a protest that left one Trump speech airing without sound. The White House had teased the channel through cryptic videos , and it went live on its YouTube account, WhiteHouse.gov and the official White House app. Reality check: Presidents have long used White House platforms to share speeches and events with the public. What we know about Trump TV How it works: The channel launched as "TRUMP TV: The Essentials Station." "Trump TV is a 24/7 livestream of the Administration's greatest hits, unfiltered," Kaelan Dorr, deputy assistant to the president, wrote on X . So far, the channel has shown curated clips of past Trump speeches and executive actions, along with live events. Catch up quick: The initial programming included Trump's July 3 Mount Rushmore speech before shifting into footage of his 2025 inauguration, per multiple reports . The Daily Beast reports 8,500 viewers were watching the stream during its first hour. Around 1,200 people were watching Tuesday afternoon as the channel aired a Trump health care announcement from August, according to an Axios review of the stream. Zoom in: The stream can also carry live events. On Tuesday, the stream carried Vice President Vance's briefing on fraud claims. But while Trump addressed the United Nations General Assembly Tuesday morning, Trump TV was replaying an earlier speech from the National Prayer Breakfast. Unanswered questions about Trump TV What we're watching: So far, Trump TV has no anchors, news ticker or headline chyrons. The stream includes banners asking viewers to text White House officials. It's unclear who staffs the channel, makes programming decisions or sets its schedule. What they're saying: A White House official tells Axios that the channel's purpose is to replay Trump's "greatest hits that the media fails to cover fairly, oftentimes on purpose." The intrigue: The White House's revamped livestream page labels its regular feed "CH 45" and Trump TV "CH 47" — references to Trump serving as the 45th and 47th president. Trump's previous streaming ventures Flashback: Trump has experimented with direct-to-audience video before. In 2016, Trump's presidential campaign launched a nightly Facebook Live show called "Trump Tower Live" that was meant to deliver campaign messaging directly to the public. Trump Media's Truth+ offers 24/7 news streams and on-demand entertainment. It appears on Truth+ apps and remains a commercial streaming service rather than an official government stream. The service began rolling out in 2024. Its lineup has included broadcasts of Newsmax, OAN and Real America's Voice.

events.title: Trailer chassis stacked vertically, 5-min EV battery swaps, smarter inventory forecasting: What modern logistics looks like in S’pore
events.summary: Enabled by innovation and with Enterprise Singapore’s support, home-grown firms build new capabilities to stay competitive as demands on the sector grow Allied Container Group managing director Lim Kian Chin (right) at one of the company’s Jurong depots, where automation and digitalisation are helping it make better use of resources. In an industrial corner of western Singapore, trailers that would normally take up individual parking lots are instead stacked side by side – upright. For Allied Container Group, this allows a single parking lot to hold as many as eight trailer chassis vertically, freeing up about 0.4 hectares of land (about the size of 10 basketball courts) for other uses. The vertical trailer parking system, developed with support from Enterprise Singapore’s (EnterpriseSG) Enterprise Development Grant (streamlined to EDGE Grant from Sept 30), is an eye-catching answer to a very Singaporean problem: how does a company continue to grow with the little land available? Allied’s vertical parking system reduces the space needed for trailer chassis parking by up to seven times, helping the haulage operator work around land constraints. Allied’s solution is to get more out of not just its land, but also its manpower and time. The home-grown logistics company has also been digitising container inspections, automating routine processes and moving workflows online. Its managing director Lim Kian Chin says: “In Singapore, you cannot simply buy more land. Operating in Singapore requires us to be relentless about efficiency.” The pressure extends across Singapore’s logistics sector. As companies seek to get more out of their resources while meeting demands for faster and more visible deliveries, improving productivity has become increasingly important. At the same time, disruptions to global supply chains have put a premium on the ability to adapt quickly. Jesse Satria Oeni, director for the logistics and mobility division at EnterpriseSG, says logistics companies must adapt as global disruptions and geopolitical tensions reconfigure global supply chains. He adds: “The transformation of our logistics ecosystem through adoption of the latest digital and automation solutions will help companies enhance their productive capacity to capture a greater share of these global goods flows.” Moving people into higher-tech roles Founded as a single-truck operation in 1975, Allied has grown into a logistics group with more than 300 full-time employees and container depots in markets such as Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand and beyond. Allied’s ground staff use its Interactive Depot Operating System (iDOS) to carry out tasks such as container inspections digitally, replacing paper-based processes. Lim, who joined his father in the family business in 1989, has long pushed for greater use of technology. That effort accelerated after Allied’s leadership team took part in EnterpriseSG’s Enterprise Leadership for Transformation programme in 2021. The programme equips business leaders with the skills to develop and carry out plans for growth and transformation. For Allied, it prompted a broader rethink of how technology could be used across its operations. Processes that once relied heavily on people and paperwork are now automated or have moved online. As the work changed, so did the jobs. Ground staff, who previously carried out manual inspections or gate processing, are trained to manage automated equipment. The company has also introduced automated seal dispensers with the support of EnterpriseSG, reducing the need for workers to handle the process manually. Such changes shift employees away from repetitive tasks towards roles that involve overseeing and operating technology. “By investing heavily in continuous learning, we are building a tech-literate workforce capable of managing sophisticated logistics tech, improving job safety, and driving overall productivity,” says Lim. How logistics firms can cut emissions without slowing deliveries Improving productivity is only one part of the transformation under way in logistics. Companies are also looking for ways to cut emissions while keeping goods moving reliably. One way is to replace diesel-powered heavy vehicles with electric ones, reducing emissions from fleets that spend long hours on the road. For heavy goods vehicles (HGV), making that switch viable for day-to-day operations means overcoming another challenge: time. Large batteries take up to four hours to charge, potentially keeping vehicles off the road for longer. Battery swapping offers one alternative: a depleted battery can be replaced with a fully charged one in about five minutes. EcoSwift director Ryan Woon (centre) with his team. The company is testing battery swapping as a way to make electric heavy vehicles more practical for logistics operators.

events.title: Microsoft disrupts AI-assisted platform that compromised 12,000 accounts
events.summary: Microsoft said Tuesday that it led an industry-wide disruption of a subscription-based scam platform that used an AI chatbot to compromise 12,000 Microsoft accounts over a few-month span. Named EvilTokens, the platform was introduced over a Telegram channel in February and charged an initial $1,500 fee and a recurring $500 charge each month after that. EvilTokens provided a single service for streamlining most steps required to compromise email accounts in large numbers. From there, the platform helped customers analyze inboxes, select targets that would provide the biggest potential payouts, and draft follow-up emails that provided realistic ruses for tricking company employees into transferring funds to attacker-controlled accounts. Minutes, not days “While EvilTokens helped cybercriminals access email accounts, at the center of the service was an AI-style chatbot that could analyze a victim’s inbox and help criminals identify trusted relationships, payment authorizations, and sensitive responsibilities, as well as other circumstances where fraud was most likely to succeed,” Microsoft said . “The platform could even recommend fraud strategies, including drafting messages that impersonated trusted contacts to help criminals trick victims into taking action.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Anthropic and OpenAI roll out cheaper models in first release since call for slowdown
events.summary: Anthropic and OpenAI announced new, less costly artificial intelligence models, as both labs face stiff competition from rivals offering open-weight models. The releases are the first from either lab since fears erupted around AI's potential threat to humanity. OpenAI introduced GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Anthropic unveiled Claude Opus 5.5. Anthropic and OpenAI on Tuesday each announced new, less costly artificial intelligence models as both frontier labs continue to face stiff competition from cheaper, open-weight competitors. OpenAI introduced additional tiers to its GPT-6 family, with GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, slashing the API prices by 50% compared with GPT-5.6 promotional pricing. Sol, which is a tier below Astra, is meant for more complex workloads like coding, while the company's Luna offering is geared toward "high-volume tasks" such as extracting information or summarizing documents, the company wrote. Anthropic unveiled Claude Opus 5.5 on Tuesday, its latest release in the new Claude 5.5 model family. The company described the latest release as a more token-efficient version that will cost around 40% less to run than the company's Opus 5. "One of the things we're continuing to innovate on is how to make that thinking, how to make the answering more efficient, so it uses less tokens depending on your effort setting," Dianne Penn, head of product management, research and labs at Anthropic, told CNBC in an interview. The separate releases are the first to roll out since Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for an industrywide slowdown on developing advanced AI as the debate about model safety reached a fever pitch in recent weeks. Former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon set off the debate when he posted to X on Sept. 8 that he had quit his job, warning that both labs were "gambling with our lives." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk also joined Amodei's call. The new releases come as OpenAI and Anthropic work to satisfy customers who are looking for more cost-effective models and seeking to rein in AI spending. The labs are facing pressure from companies offering cheaper, open-weight models, including Chinese firms Alibaba, Moonshot AI and DeepSeek — CNBC's Kate Rooney contributed to this report. events.title: Fintech startups that hated banks are now becoming them
events.summary: Liz’s view “This is the beginning of a bankless world,” proclaimed a 2016 ad for SoFi, which embodied the sneering disdain its generation of fintech startups had for the banks they were out to dethrone. SoFi is now a bank, the 46th biggest in America. So are Klarna and PayPal. Chime is the latest to bite the bullet, announcing the acquisition of a bank earlier this month. Revolut, whose CEO was once quoted saying “I just don’t like banks,” has also applied for a license. Block, which got a skinny banking license in 2021, wants another one . Contempt for banks was hard-coded into these companies’ DNA. Now they all want to be one. Why? First, the real money to be made in financial services is in lending, especially as the young tech-savvy customers they courted through YOLO brokerage, crypto trading, and money transfers grow up and want to buy a house. In the lending business, controlling your funding is important, and there’s no cheaper funding in the world than savings accounts. Relying on bank partners to fund the loans you want to make is risky, as LendingClub found out the hard way , which is why it bought a bank in 2020 and is now a full-fledged bank called Happen. These companies’ pivots are also an acknowledgement that their hypergrowth stage is over. Regulators don’t like banks growing too quickly because they tend to screw up when they do , which is why Robinhood abandoned its pursuit of a license in 2019. A reminder: We had “Robinhood becomes a bank” on our 2026 Semafor Business bingo card . We might be early, but I don’t think we’re wrong. Notable Chime shares jumped on the news of its acquisition of Stride , but have since sunk nearly 10%.

events.title: Good news for people whose jobs are being reshaped by AI
events.summary: For jobs with more AI exposure, median advertised pay has grown 46% since 2021. Maskot/Getty Images AI is changing which skills employers value. A report from Indeed Hiring Lab showed which jobs have seen higher advertised pay growth since 2021. Jobs that are more likely to be reshaped by AI have seen greater gains. If you're looking for a job that's ripe to be reshaped by AI, you are likely seeing better pay advertised than just a few years ago. Indeed Hiring Lab grouped jobs more exposed to AI together and found that this category has seen pay growth skyrocket since 2021, more so than those less exposed to AI. Jobs more exposed to AI are more likely to have skills done or transformed by AI, including: Software development IT systems and support Data and analytics Marketing Banking and finance Economist Jack Kennedy said that AI is "reshaping which skills the market pays for" rather than replacing skilled workers. The report showed median advertised salary for more AI-exposed jobs has surged by 46% since 2021. Pay for less-exposed jobs grew by 25%, a slowdown from a year ago. These included: Nursing Personal care and home health Food preparation and service Cleaning and sanitation Production and manufacturing There's a larger gap based on where people are in the career ladder. The pay growth gap between more- and less-AI-exposed jobs is barely noticeable for entry-level roles , unlike for more senior roles. Kennedy said jobs that are more AI-exposed have also generally experienced a rebound in job opportunities over the past year. "Solid growth in postings over the past year, alongside rising pay, is consistent with the skills in these roles becoming more valuable," he said. Separately, the Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes annual job projections that show how hundreds of jobs could change over a decade. This year, the government agency also classified how exposed jobs are to AI, drawing on a few studies about AI. Many of the 206 very highly exposed jobs were high-paying and projected to see employment increase between 2025 and 2035, such as software developers and management analysts. Meanwhile, physician assistants and dental hygienists are high-paying, low AI-exposure jobs projected to grow. Some think AI will lead to the end. Jacob Coxon, who worked for AI research employers OpenAI and Anthropic, wrote on X earlier this month that he resigned from Anthropic and that "people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade. " More Americans think it will, at the very least, mean fewer jobs are needed. A Pew Research Center survey found that 71% of US adults think AI will mean fewer jobs in the country over the next two decades, up from 64% who said this in 2024. "Worries tend to run particularly high in countries with higher gross domestic product per capita," a new Pew Research Report said. Seventy-six percent of people in both Australia and South Korea believe it will lead to fewer jobs. While there are fears about AI's capabilities, some are embracing ways to leverage it at work, such as automating and speeding up tasks. Some are also incorporating it into their daily lives. A new personal AI agent from Meta topped the free apps list on Apple's US App Store. Some people use AI chatbots for relationship and other advice. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Beijing and Washington talk about an AI hotline. But who will answer the call?
events.summary: Hello and welcome to Eye on AI. In this edition: Anthropic and OpenAI both release new, cheaper AI models. U.S. President Donald Trump creates an “AI Force.” China and the U.S. agree to discuss an AI incident hotline. Microsoft executive called OpenAI training on publishers’ copyrighted works “the largest theft of labor in history.” AI scientists are making good progress. And the AI safety researchers are not all right.  Before we get to today’s AI news—please consider joining me at the inaugural Fortune AIQ Summit at the New York Stock Exchange on Oct. 1: Spend the afternoon with senior executives from companies on the Fortune AIQ 75 list and explore how you can scale your AI experimentation and translate investments into measurable business value. I will be leading discussions alongside co-hosts, Fortune Editor-in-Chief Alyson Shontell and Live Media Editorial Director Andrew Nusca. Apply here to attend . Ok, so today’s newsletter is a bit of a potpourri. All eyes this week, will be on the talks between U.S. President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in Washington. We know AI governance is on the agenda of that meeting, which takes place Thursday, but that’s about all we know. My colleague Emily Forlini wrote a piece last week on why the Trump-Xi meeting is unlikely to result in any kind of international agreement to slow the pace of AI development or create an agreed framework for controlling the technology. It’s worth a read. That said, there was an inkling that these two AI superpowers might, in fact, be able to agree to a few basics. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent emerged Sunday from meetings with a Chinese delegation led by Vice Premier He Lifeng that took place at the headquarters of JP Morgan in New York and announced that the two sides had agreed to hold further talks about setting up a hotline to notify one another of AI incidents that created national security concerns. What exactly this means in practice is unclear. But as Bessent told reporters, “moving from opaque to more transparency between the number one and number two AI powers in the world is very important.” Such hotlines have historically helped ease tensions between rivals. At the very least, they might prevent some sort of accidental incident caused by AI from tripping over into armed conflict, or even nuclear war. There are already signs that such AI-triggered accidents are possible: just this weekend, CNN reported that earlier this year the U.S. military almost attempted to seize a Chinese ship in the Middle East that an AI-generated intelligence report had suggested was carrying nuclear weapons components to Iran. The intelligence had been generated by an AI model that fused secret U.S. intelligence with open-source data. The only problem is that the model’s conclusion was an AI “hallucination”—and the error was caught only after the U.S. had launched aircraft carrying armed personnel who were preparing to intercept the Chinese vessel. Had the error not been spotted in time, it could have led to a diplomatic incident—or far worse. But while a hotline might prevent this kind of incident from spiraling into war between the U.S. and China, it is less clear whether it would do anything to help the world avoid or contain a “loss of control” incident involving an advanced AI system that goes rogue. Phoning a friend ain’t gonna help For instance, what if one country (or companies based there) creates an AI that goes rogue and starts hacking banks around the globe? And what if that AI copies itself on servers around the world, making it difficult to shut down without shutting down large parts of the internet? While notifying the other country about this is nice—it might help them take some action to secure their financial infrastructure before too much damage is done—it isn’t clear exactly what the country receiving the heads up is supposed to do. As AI safety researchers keep warning, the world hasn’t figured out a good way to guarantee that AI models adhere to human intentions and values. And neither the U.S. or China has enacted any rules requiring AI models to have some sort of “kill switch.” Nor is it even clear that an effective kill switch can even be built. So sure, this is a promising, baby step towards some sort of AI governance agreement between the U.S. and China. But there’s also a long history of hotlines failing to evolve into any kind of lasting diplomatic resolution. Right now, the Washington-Beijing AI hotline is a lot like agreeing to build the “Bat Sign” before Batman exists. You can flash it into the sky, but no caped crusader is coming to save us. Why the hack of OpenAI should worry every company Another big piece of AI news from last week was the revelation , first reported in the Wall Street Journal , that a small team of white hat hackers had used Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5 model to hack into the community-message platform Discourse and from there to compromise the ChatGPT account of an OpenAI employee. Once they had access to that account, they were able to use it to also access and alter software sitting on a repository where OpenAI stored a lot of its sensitive code. Coming amid the raging debate about the best way to prevent “rogue AI” incidents, many cybersecurity experts jumped on the incident to make the case that the real issue is not so much that AI is increasingly uncontrollable, but that leading AI companies have horribly lax security. It’s not just OpenAI. Anthropic has also had embarrassing security lapses too. It was ironic, many critics pointed out, that both companies are using the threat of AI-powered cyber attacks as part of a marketing pitch for customers to use their most advanced (and expensive) AI models to secure their networks before the bad guys get to them, but neither seems to have yet done a very good job of doing that themselves. The incident also highlighted a couple of uncomfortable truths. One is that AI agents running inside companies are a great target for hackers. Making these AI agents useful often means giving them access to lots of other tools and data sources, many of which contain sensitive corporate information or control key business processes. If hackers can gain access to and take command of these agents, they can do a lot of damage very quickly. To cybersecurity experts, the answer is to lock these AI agents down, and to operate based on “zero trust” principals. Treat every AI agent as a potential insider threat. Give the agents access only to the data they need to complete a task—preferably with using a “just-in-time, just enough access” methodology, where permissions need to be renewed every time the agent needs to access a database or make a tool call. But a lot of zero trust methods potentially make AI agents a lot less useful. events.title: IDB president says ‘we need to look’ at Venezuela
events.summary: The News The head of the Inter-American Development Bank said Tuesday the lender is weighing a return to Venezuela after nearly a decade away, but did not say whether Caracas’ unpaid debts would be forgiven. “As a development bank, we need to look at Venezuela and look at the Venezuelan people and see if there’s an opportunity for us to engage,” IDB President Ilan Goldfajn said at Semafor’s The Next 3 Billion, adding that talks on a formal engagement plan are already underway. Asked about whether the IDB would seek repayment of Venezuela’s doubts, Goldfajn said only that it was “part of the conversation.” The bank halted new loans in 2018 after Venezuela fell behind on its payments, leaving roughly $2 billion outstanding; a planned re-engagement would focus on electricity and social protection , according to Reuters. The future governance of Venezuela was thrown into doubt after US forces captured President Nicolás Maduro in Caracas in January. His former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, has since taken over as acting president. Under pressure from Washington, Rodríguez has shifted foreign and economic policy, and some foreign companies and firms are now moving to invest or expand in the country. It’s unclear, however, whether the US military operation will ultimately tip the country toward democratic reform. Know More Goldfajn also spoke at length about the region’s treatment of AI, describing the Latin American leaders he met on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly as “hopeful, but with eyes wide open” when it comes to the fast-moving technology. He also warned that Latin American leaders are cognizant of the risk of falling far behind in AI adoption and development. “It’s not that we are behind in the race, we’re not even in the race,” he said, summing up the views of leaders he has spoken to about the issue.

events.title: How to get your boss and coworkers on board with your idea
events.summary: Instead of trying to convince someone why your argument is the right one, find a reason why they should care. SimpleImages/Getty Images Today's tip to get better at work: Get others to support your ideas by appealing to their interests. Showing someone how they can benefit from your pitch is an effective way to persuade them. Write down all the reasons your idea could help the person you're asking before you present it. Get better at: Persuading others Today's move If you want to get your boss or colleague on board with an idea , think about what they care about and frame the pitch around that. Why it works Amanda Nimon-Peters, a leadership professor and author of "Working With Influence," said that people often resort to using rational arguments when they want to persuade someone else. While you may have strong reasons for why the other person should be invested, you may be better off appealing to their interests. Nimon-Peters said persuasion isn't about getting people to do things they don't want to do; it's about finding ways to make the outcome and success that you're after also appealing to them. Try it today Before you talk to the person you need to convince at work, write down the answer to this question: "What's in it for them?" Maybe your idea or pitch saves them time, maybe it makes their job easier, or it creates a solution to a problem they've been frustrated with. Then center your pitch around that. The bottom line Research suggests that rational arguments aren't the only effective strategy for persuading others . A 2017 report published in The Leadership Quarterly analyzed 49 studies on how people influence others at work. It found that rational arguments can work, but other approaches, like showing someone what they stand to gain, were also linked to positive outcomes. Instead of proving that you're right, you should try to show the person why they should care. Source This insight is drawn from Business Insider reporting on how to be more persuasive at work, citing advice from Amanda Nimon-Peters, a behavioral science professor who studies influence. Read the full story here. This story also includes data published in "Leadership Quarterly," about influence tactics. You can view the report here . How do you convince your boss or colleagues to support your ideas at work? We want to hear your best persuasion techniques in the comments below. events.title: Meta admits Muse’s likeness to OpenClaw isn’t a coincidence
events.summary: Disrupt 2026: OpenAI, Anthropic, Replit, and more take over 6 industry stages. 25% off tickets now Disrupt ticket savings of up to $200 + 50% off a second ends Sept 25, 11:59 p.m. PT. REGISTER HERE. Early adopters of Meta’s Muse have been speculating that the reason the AI works so well is because it’s OpenClaw under the hood, wrapped in a more consumer-friendly package. Meta now says those comparisons aren’t entirely off-base. According to an X post by Nat Friedman, head of product at Meta’s Superintelligence Labs (MSL), Muse was “definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw.” However, he clarified that Muse itself was “built from scratch.” Friedman, the former GitHub CEO who joined Meta last year alongside Meta’s Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang , said that the team at Meta had fallen in love with OpenClaw and wanted Muse to be “something like OpenClaw” that could be scaled to billions of people. Because OpenClaw is an open source project, it wouldn’t be surprising that Meta looked to it for inspiration, especially given its breakout success , which prompted OpenAI to snatch up its creator earlier this year. However, it speaks to Meta’s well-known playbook that involves taking promising products, then copying their best features — something it did most notoriously with Snapchat’s invention of the stories format. Friedman’s statement on X was made in response to a post that had gone viral among the AI crowd, where Ansh Nanda , an AI app co-founder, claimed that “Muse is LITERALLY OpenClaw for normies.” Nanda’s X post had included a conversation with Muse, where the AI agent said that the similarity between its own system files and those belonging to OpenClaw was not just “a coincidence” but rather “a match.” Soon, this thread (and X more broadly) began blowing up as others shared their own comparisons and findings. For instance, one person pointed out that Muse also had a SOUL.md file, the plain text configuration file (written in a simple formatting language called Markdown) that defines an AI agent’s personality, communication style and tone, values, behavioral boundaries, and expertise. A third noted that the files weren’t just named the same between the two assistants; their content was almost entirely the same. Following his X post, Friedman also responded to a question about why Muse had copied the exact file names that made up the AI agent’s workspace and had “nearly identical content” for the SOUL.md file. Instead of disputing these claims, Friedman simply replied that “we thought that Peter [Steinberger, OpenClaw’s creator] got those things exactly right.” “We built Muse from scratch, but it is definitely heavily inspired as a product by OpenClaw. After I used OpenClaw in January, I bought hundreds of Mac minis for the MSL team, and lots of us fell in love with using OpenClaw (and other personal agents), Friedman said on X. (TechCrunch has corrected Friedman’s punctuation for readability.) “@steipete [Peter Steinberger] is a genius, and his harness was pioneering from the jump. I think a lot of people were inspired by it. Our goal with Muse was to build something like OpenClaw that we could make safe and secure and easy to use and scale to billions of people,” he wrote. The Muse app has been something of a hit so far, having recently hit No. 1 on the U.S. App Store. Data indicates that it’s now outpacing ChatGPT’s launch when the platforms and market availability are compared directly. Reached for comment, a Meta spokesperson pointed to Friedman’s statement, saying the company had nothing more to add beyond that. events.title: Keyed in: UAE dirham symbol makes debut in Unicode 18.0
events.summary: UAE's dirham symbol has officially been included in Unicode 's version 18.0, making it easier for computer and smartphone makers to include it on keyboards. Unicode, based in California , is the technology industry’s leading organisation for standardising emojis and digital characters across billions of digital devices. Last week, the organisation described the UAE dirham symbol as "among the most anticipated new characters" in version 18.0, along with the Omani riyal and the Maldivian rufiyaa. Before users go looking for the UAE dirham symbol , however, they should note that it is up to tech companies to adopt the latest Unicode update. But the fact that the dirham made it past Unicode's beta version and into the final iteration means it will soon be a lot easier to select that symbol on devices. "Each of these symbols was authorised for public use by the respective monetary authority over a year ago, but usage has been hindered by lack of a standardised encoding," a Unicode blog entry reads. "With the release of Unicode 18.0, vendors are now able to implement support for these symbols." The organisation's core specification document, with more than 1,100 pages, provides more insight on the UAE dirham's journey to being standardised for keyboards. "UAE Dirham sign was unveiled by the Central Bank of the United Arab Emirates on March 27, 2025, as the official currency symbol for the UAE dirham," the document reads. "It incorporates two horizontal lines that embody the financial and monetary stability of the UAE dirham, and which are also inspired by the UAE flag." The dirham symbol has been given U+20C3 as the code point identifier by Unicode to assist programmers in encoding the symbol within devices and software. Last year, shortly after the UAE Central Bank announced the creation of the symbol as part of a drive to bolster the country's position as a global financial centre, the bank applied to Unicode to have its presence on technology platforms. “We confirm that the proposed glyph is original, it does not use a specific font and as such does not require any licensing to allow its inclusion in the official Unicode charts,” the UAE's submission letter read. “The symbol is intended for the general public, businesses and government in everyday life for transactions and represents the country's national currency.” In a blog post in February, Unicode said that monetary authorities introducing new symbols for their currencies represented a “significant milestone for financial and commercial activity in their domain”. “The consortium is honoured to work with monetary authorities, and would like to help make the launch of a new symbol as smooth as possible,” Unicode said. The UAE Central Bank released a style guideline in 2025 detailing how it envisions the dirham symbol appearing on the number 6 key on keyboard layouts. Ultimately, that will also be up to keyboard makers. Meanwhile, the Unicode Consortium, which has existed since 1991, implied that the currency symbol additions were just the tip of the iceberg in version 18.0. "This version adds 13,007 new characters, including nine new emoji characters, as well as many other characters and symbols, bringing the total number of encoded characters to 172,808," Unicode said.

events.title: Trump slams Iran and Cuba, defends AI growth in boastful UN speech
events.summary: President Donald Trump focused on a wide range of threats the U.S. faces from abroad during an address to the United Nations General Assembly. Trump defended his decision to launch a war against Iran and slammed Cuba as a "failed state." He also touted a new military deal with Greenland and Denmark. President Donald Trump on Tuesday focused on a wide range of threats the U.S. faces from abroad during a frequently boastful address to the United Nations General Assembly in Manhattan. Trump, in a roughly 37-minute speech, also directly criticized the U.N. itself, and reaffirmed his view that the U.S. artificial intelligence industry should continue its rapid growth with few restraints or guardrails. Trump defended his decision to launch a war against Iran , accusing the Islamic Republic of seeking to erect a defensive missile arsenal before making a "mad dash to a nuclear bomb." As the war approaches its eighth month with no clear end in sight, Trump said he is poised to make a "big decision" on whether to make a deal or quickly "annihilate" the country. He then predicted once again that a deal will be made "right after" the Nov. 3 midterm elections , claiming "it doesn't make sense for them not to." "They're waiting to see how I do in the midterm election," he said. "What they don't realize is that I'm not running." "I gave absolutely no credence and will not give credence to the election when it comes to Iran. It doesn't even enter my mind. The only thing that does is that Iran will never have a nuclear weapon," Trump said. At a bilateral meeting with United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham after the speech, Trump added that he believes global energy prices, which have shot up due to the war and created upward inflation pressure, will retreat right after the conflict ends. "I think as soon as the war's over, the numbers are going to come way down," Trump said, adding, "pricing generally, because oil is the big thing." In his address, Trump also touted a military deal with Greenland and Denmark, saying it gives the U.S. "the complete ability to do what is necessary to defend the American continent, and also Europe and other places." That agreement was signed at a trilateral meeting later Tuesday morning. Trump called Cuba an "absolutely failed state" and accused it of "coordinating with left-wing radicals and Communist networks" in the U.S. "Communism will never be coming to America, but freedom will be coming to Cuba," Trump told the assembled leaders. He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio is in negotiations with the island nation. As he spoke, the Cuban delegation stood up and left the hall. The Cuban Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "The United States will no longer permit threats to America to gain a foothold anywhere in the Western Hemisphere," Trump said, pointing to his administration's intervention in Venezuela this year as proof. "And if necessary, we will use our unmatched military might to secure the vital national interests of the United States," he said. Trump administration advances $24.3 billion F-35 deal to Saudi Arabia Bill to curb AI data center utility costs hits snag in Senate House heads home to campaign amid calls for urgent AI action Toward the end of the speech, Trump turned to AI — first by debuting his attempt to rebrand it "super intelligence" and also whipsawing on the U.S. government's role in putting guardrails on the technology. The president then compared those raising concerns about AI — a group that includes some tech leaders — with those warning about climate change, which Trump also denies is a problem. "These are the same people that are now saying that AI is going to kill us all, that robots are going to attack us, and that everything is going to be a total disaster," Trump said. He reiterated his view that winning the race for AI superiority is the key to U.S. global dominance. "That's the group that wins, and we're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," he said. "We're going to keep it very, very straight and very strong. I'm not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution." The government will "rein things in" if needed and will lead the sector "safely and responsibly," Trump said. But he also said, "We will only encourage superintelligence. We're going to encourage it, not rein it in."

events.title: Data centre funding surges to record $35b despite AI 'bubble' risks
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Data centre funding surges to record $35b this year despite AI 'bubble' risks Data centre financing is accelerating at breakneck speed. ( ABC News: Billy Cooper ) A Reserve Bank staff note reveals Australian data centre operators have raised a record sum of at least $35 billion so far this year. Funding obtained by Australian-focused operators has increased 46 per cent from 2025. The amount of capital being raised can provide early indications of how much more construction is coming. Australian data centre operators have raised record capital of at least $35 billion so far this year, as the rapid construction of AI infrastructure has become an increasingly important part of the country's business investment growth. A new Reserve Bank staff note obtained exclusively by the ABC shows funding obtained by Australian-focused operators had already surpassed the $24 billion raised across all of 2025, an increase of 46 per cent. The research marks the first time an analyst from the RBA has estimated how much money has been raised to build Australian data centres. The analysis covers Airtrunk, CDC, Firmus, Goodman, Macquarie Technology and subsidiaries of Stack Infrastructure and Equinix. It draws on financing across syndicated lending, bonds, public and private equity as well as some private transactions. Bigger and hungrier: What we know about 27 proposed new data centres Dozens of approved but yet-to-be-built AI data centre projects are expected to escape the federal government's proposed restrictions around energy and water use. This year's funding is also more than seven times the annual average recorded between 2020 and 2024, highlighting the breakneck speed at which financing for the sector has accelerated. However, the rapid growth is coming off a low base. Data centre operators still account for only 16 per cent of funding raised by Australian "non-financial corporates" across the markets captured by the analysis. The author of the note, RBA analyst Bradley Speed, states the $35 billion figure was conservative because the data does not capture all single-bank loans and may also miss some private transactions. Michele Bullock says "AI is the great white hope to improve productivity," but it is coming with a short-term headache. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) One reason the note examines data centre financing is because the amount of capital being raised can provide early indications of how much more construction is coming. Mr Speed said funding could provide a "useful leading indicator for data centre investment in Australia", because local operators tend to rely on external capital to fund large construction programs. This comes as the RBA grapples with how to respond to the AI investment boom, which is contributing to Australia's high inflation problem. Building data centres requires huge amounts of spending on construction, electrical infrastructure and skilled labour, as well as imported equipment such as advanced chips and servers. As the data centre boom increases demand for workers and resources in an already stretched construction sector, it means those resources could, relatively speaking, become more expensive and add to inflationary pressures elsewhere in the economy. Governor Michele Bullock said on Tuesday that while AI investment was already adding to demand, there were "very few signs yet" that it was boosting the economy's supply capacity. "So we've got this sort of awkward sequencing event at the moment where, in Australia at least, we are in a situation of excess demand and the AI boom is adding to that demand ahead of any potential supply impacts that it might have going forward," she said. The governor also said central banks globally were watching the risk of an AI investment bubble and the potential consequences if it unwound in a disorderly way. The RBA's August meeting minutes showed the board had discussed the possibility of the AI and data centre investment boom becoming larger than anticipated, which runs the risk of driving inflation higher. The RBA analyst note shows the boom is being financed overwhelmingly through borrowing money. Debt accounted for 85 per cent of new funding obtained by Australian data centre operators so far in 2026, slightly above estimates of 60 to 80 per cent in the United States. The biggest source has been syndicated lending, in which a group of lenders combines to provide a single, often large, loan.

The hackers made the claim on their dark web leak site, which TechCrunch reviewed, saying they had stolen “sensitive data on almost all FBI agents and individuals who filed an application with the FBI for a job.” 404 Media first reported on the breach after receiving a sample of the stolen names, home addresses, and phone numbers of FBI agents and their spouses, and verifying a portion of the stolen data against public records. The hackers say their hack is “not financially motivated,” and are demanding that the FBI remove a report that they say contains false allegations about the group. The independent publication said the hackers breached an Oracle PeopleSoft server, often used by human resources and recruiters to store job applicants’ personal information, then pivoted to breach an Amazon-hosted government cloud storing the agents and applicants’ data. ShinyHunters told the publication that they took terabytes of data but did not say what they would do with the information if the FBI does not take down its published report. The stolen data could present a major counterintelligence threat, in which hackers and overseas spies use the information to coerce or extort FBI agents and their families into cooperating with a foreign government. The hackers reportedly defaced the FBI’s jobs site, which showed at the time of publication that the portal was “currently down for maintenance.” The site also said that the FBI’s special agent applicant portal was also down. The FBI did not respond to a request for comment about the incident on Tuesday, and neither did the ShinyHunters hackers. This is the second known breach of an FBI system this year after unidentified hackers broke into one of the agency’s systems for managing real-time wiretaps and foreign intelligence-gathering warrants, which could have identified targets of the agency’s surveillance. Separately, FBI director Kash Patel also had his personal email account hacked and leaked by an Iran-backed hacking group called Handala in retaliation for U.S.-led strikes against Iran. events.title: I only shop for 2, but buying in bulk saves me money. Here are 10 things I always get at Costco.
events.summary: Food and household staples are some of the things I buy in bulk at Costco. Rebecca Kaplan I'm a longtime Costco shopper who buys items in bulk for my household of two. I always stock up on staples like toilet paper, laundry detergent, and dishwasher detergent. Items like eggs, chicken nuggets, canned tuna, and white bread always make it into my cart. I've been a Costco shopper for as long as I can remember. As a kid, I often went there with my parents on the weekends to buy bulk food items, books, clothing, and Barbie dolls — and of course, enjoy a $1.50 hot dog and soda combination for lunch. Now, as an adult, I shop there for bulk staples for my household of two. These are the 10 items that always make it into my shopping cart. Prices may vary by location. Kirkland Signature toilet paper is a must. Rebecca Kaplan Paper goods can be expensive at my local supermarket, but at Costco, I find they're a great deal. Although I pay a little more to buy name-brand paper towels, I do purchase Kirkland Signature toilet paper. As a household of two people with stomach issues, we're picky about what toilet paper we buy. However, I think the Kirkland Signature version is comparable to the Angel Soft brand. During my most recent trip, I paid $25 for 30 rolls. Eggs are a great deal at Costco. Rebecca Kaplan When the average price for a dozen eggs rose to a record-high $6.23 in early 2025, I turned to Costco for more cost-effective options. Now, I typically buy the 24-count of large white eggs for $4.83 and use them for breakfast, a snack, and a key ingredient when baking. I always stock up on laundry detergent. Rebecca Kaplan Another one of my Costco staples is laundry detergent . The warehouse carries a variety of brands, including sensitive skin options, which I prefer. During this trip, I grabbed a container of Tide Free and Gentle Pods. Dishwasher detergent is a steal, too. Rebecca Kaplan I also stock up on dishwasher detergent at Costco, which is typically stocked in both liquid and pod forms. I grabbed the Cascade Complete pods, which were on sale for $14, which I thought was a great deal. My husband loves the Kirkland Signature canned tuna. Rebecca Kaplan My husband loves canned tuna and says that the Kirkland Signature albacore solid white version is better than other brands he's had. He eats it on a sandwich mixed with mayonnaise or on its own with crackers. Chicken nuggets always land a spot in my cart. Rebecca Kaplan As a picky eater, I eat chicken nuggets several times a week. I like to make the Dino Buddies version in the toaster oven and have them with a side of rice or pasta. I love looking for novelty and seasonal items. Rebecca Kaplan Some of my shopping is dependent on what's currently available seasonally, or what novelty items are in stock. On this shopping trip, I grabbed the Reese's-inspired One-brand protein bars. My husband tries to consume as much protein as possible and loves Reese's, so these were a quick yes. White bread is another item I like to buy in bulk. Rebecca Kaplan I eat a peanut butter sandwich almost every day for lunch, so you can imagine how quickly we go through bread. Costco carries Pepperidge Farm white bread as a two-pack, so I always grab that — especially because the cost for two loaves ($6.37) is similar to what I've seen for one at other supermarkets. I always search the aisles for fun drinks. Rebecca Kaplan Drinks are another item that usually come home with me. I like to put some tomato sauce on it for another easy way to increase our protein and fiber intake. Curious to know what other shoppers put in their carts? Check out our other Costco diaries here. events.title: a16z is challenging Silicon Valley’s love for drop-outs by launching a school
